speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: STATEMENTS ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend is
quite right: I did take a note or two, because he covered quite a number of subjects, and it was pretty difficult to keep them all in mind. However, I think there are only one or two to which I need refer.
First, the reference of my hon. friend to Mr. Dunning. I have no knowledge whatever of the matter of the Canadian Pacific railway stock to which he refers, except, that as I remember it, my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) stated the other night that there had been no mention or suggestion of a purchase of Canadian Pacific stock. It would seem to me that probably that was a sufficient answer.
At the same time, I do feel that this practice which my hon. friend has adopted, of making this house the sounding board for any grievances which he has against citizens of Canada, must be taken notice of, at least to the extent of one saying a word for those who cannot speak for themselves.
All I want to say in this connection is, that, regardless of what is my hon. friend's opinion of Mr. Dunning, and regardless of the insinuations which he has made, I believe I shall receive general approbation from the people of Canada when I say that no citizen who has been in public life was held in higher esteem by the people of Canada generally than the gentleman whom he has attacked this afternoon. Through many years of fine public service, in the legislature of Saskatchewan, as Minister of Railways, and as Minister of Finance in the government of Canada, Mr. Dunning stands in need of no encomiums from me. My purpose is simply to take notice of the fact that he has been attacked this afternoon. I know that citizens generally will feel, as I do, that the attack is entirely
unwarranted, is quite out of place, and that the subject regarding which Mr. Dunning's name has been introduced is not a matter with which the time of this house need be taken up, especially at this particular stage of the session.
The hon. member asked a question with regard to my trip overseas. May I tell him that I did not go over there to settle financial questions. I do not recall that a single financial question was discussed when I was in Great Britain, although there may have been one or two financial matters incidental to the subjects with which I was dealing. What I did go to England for, as I endeavoured to tell the house when I came back, was to see the troops over there, to consult with the commanders in the field, to meet General McNaugbton and his officers and men, to discuss the matter of organization with Canadian military headquarters, and to ascertain what further we could do in connection with our pledge to help in the war to the limit of our ability. I endeavoured to carry out these purposes. In doing so I interviewed from time to time quite a number of members of the British government and staff officials, and discussed fully what Canada might do to render further assistance. I have given, I believe, quite a full account of that to the people of this country and to the house, and I do not propose to take up time this afternoon in rehearsing it.
The hon. member mentioned another gentleman who is not here to answer for himself- Colonel Magee. He suggested that Colonel Magee was taken on the staff of the Department of National Defence as a financial adviser. Let me tell him that I occupied the position of Minister of Finance for about nine months. If I had wanted financial advisers, I can think of very few whom I would rather have had, from the point of view of finance and business, than Colonel Magee. But I do not recall having even talked with Colonel Magee when I was Minister of Finance, because assistance of that kind was not what I wanted. I may, of course, have met him on the street, but that is all. When I came to the Department of National Defence, however, last fall, I looked around for a citizen of Canada who had had some experience in connection with military matters, and who could be relied upon as having the confidence of his fellow citizens, and I found him in Colonel Magee, a man who had raised a battalion, who had taken that battalion overseas, and who had rendered sterling service in England and in France with the fourth Canadian division. Following that, Colonel



Supply-The War-Mr. Ralston
Magee came home and took a special interest in connection with training: I believe he is one of the men who was chiefly responsible for the success of the officers' training corps in Montreal. The result was that I asked Colonel Magee to come to Ottawa in the capacity of executive assistant. He accepted, and I was glad of it. I believe I shall have the approval of hon. members generally when I say that no man could have filled that position more worthily and unselfishly or more acceptably to members of the house and to all the people with whom he has come in contact. He has not been called upon to advise upon a single financial matter of any kind or description in connection with the Department of National Defence. His services have been exercised purely in connection with matters of military administration training and the many details which come up from time to time in the department in connection with which his experience and knowledge of military matters can be of advantage.
My hon. friend made some remark to the effect that I have said that we were not to send any more men overseas. I do not know where he gets that statement. It does not appear in Hansard nor in any other published statement of mine, and I am satisfied1 that I can say without reservation of any kind that I never made such a statement in my life. The argument, therefore, which my hon. friend based on that is totally fallacious. I stated when I came home that we would be sending men overseas. I have stated frequently that we have been sending men overseas. When my hon. friend asserts that somebody said that Britain did not need men but needed munitions, any statement of that kind was based on the knowledge that Canada had pledged the various formations whose dispatch overseas this house has approved as part of Canada's contribution and that that pledge would be kept.
With regard to this man Mr. McKerlie: I never saw him. As a matter of fact I know nothing whatever about him, except that two long questions were asked concerning him in the house, and the department got the answers from the files. My hon. friend may make any statement with regard to that which he sees fit. But I know that Mr. McKerlie was recommended to the responsible officers concerned by Colonel Sherman, who I understand was in charge of the ordnance training centre at that time. He was recommended first with relation to the job which he at first filled, and the title of which I have forgotten, and afterwards to be director of training at the new trade training school because he was regarded as having the technical knowledge necessary for the position. The officers who

had charge of that organization are the officers responsible for making that recommendation, and Mr. McKerlie took up his new position in connection with that work. I do not believe that he is with the department at the present time. As a matter of fact-this will probably bring another outburst from my hon. friend

I think he is in the department of my colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) at the present time-I do not know just in what capacity.
I had not intended to speak at this length, but I felt it was due to these gentlemen that I should say what I have said.

examination that in some districts the local committees are just getting underway now. I attended a meeting which one of the members was good enough to call the other night in one particular district where they were making plans less than a week ago. Yesterday was the biggest day we have had in recruiting since the call was made, and I am advised that the momentum is increasing. That is as regards recruiting.
The other question was asked by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) with reference to transportation of soldiers. I intended to make a statement in this regard on my estimates, but since the question was asked I would request the house to listen to the statement now.
A request was made in this house some time ago when the war appropriation bill was discussed that consideration be given to some amelioration of conditions in connection with fares charged soldiers, particularly on embarkation leave. That is what was referred to especially, although the request in some instances went so far as to include free transportation for soldiers on all leave. As an alternative to that there was a discussion with regard to the possibility of giving free transportation for a limited distance; that is to say, giving a zone rate or free transportation within a certain area so as to cut down expenses for those who have to travel long distances. There was a third suggestion which I promised to take up, and that was consultation with the railways to see if some substantial reduction could not be made in fares for soldiers, at least for embarkation leave, and possibly annual leave as well. I stated then, and I think I am correct, that the only occasion on which free transportation was granted in the last war was when troops were proceeding on harvest leave, and that was granted only in 1915 and 1916, and affected only the first three hundred miles.
I said at the time that the pay and allowances of soldiers was larger in this war than in the last, that the value of the dollar was greater in this war than in the last, and that these circumstances had to be taken into consideration in connection with the question of transportation. I undertook to consult the railways, however, and we have consulted them. All three ministers representing the defence services have been in consultation with the railway executives with the result that, I believe, an arrangement has been arrived at which the house will regard as meeting the situation.
There has been a misapprehension with regard to the present rates which men pay

Supply-The War-Mr. Ralston
when going on leave. The public in travelling on the railways get a return fare not for a single fare, not for fare and a half, but for double fare less 10 per cent. Under the present rates the soldiers get a return fare for a single fare. The popular conception is that the return fare is based on three cents a mile one way or one and a half cents a mile both ways, a soldier paying one fare to make the trip there and back. That assumption is not correct. The railway fares are based on competitive rates, and there are many instances in which the fare is not three cents a mile one way or one and a half cents return. Moreover, the soldier can take advantage of excursion rates the same as anyone else.
Let me give a sample or two of the mileage rates in force at the present time available to soldiers. From Halifax to Vancouver the rate is not one and a half cents; as I have said, the soldier would get a trip to Vancouver for a single fare. That does not amount to one and a half cents but to 1*03. From Montreal to Vancouver it is 1-03 and from Debert to Montreal l'Ofi a mile. Debert to Winnipeg is 1-1 a mile; Sussex to Quebec, 1-03; Sussex to Toronto, M0; Montreal to Winnipeg, 1-18; Borden to Winnipeg, 1 -05. The only case I see on this partial list in which the full one and a half cents is payable is from Borden to Montreal.
These are some examples to show the rates paid by the soldier for railway fares at the present time. I have here table after table showing what the rates are from almost any point to any other point. But I think I can say that the average charge to soldiers under the present arrangements is not more than one and a quarter cents for the whole mileage there and back, or two and a half cents for the one-way mileage.
In the discussion with the railways we had particularly in mind the matter of embarkation leave, but we felt we should take up annual leave as well. We had a consultation with the railways by the ministers of the three service departments and their officers, and this is the arrangement which has been arrived at, which will give a very substantial benefit to sailors, soldiers and airmen. As I have said, the rates average about one and a quarter cents; some are below one cent. Speaking generally the effect of the arrangement which has been made is that in respect of annual leave and embarkation leave the soldier will pay only one-third of that low rate; the remaining two-thirds will be contributed equally by the government and the railway. That is the general arrangement. The railways are knocking off one-third, the government pays one-third and the soldier pays

one-third, which means that in the case of a fare of 1-03 cents a mile the soldier pays about a third of a cent a mile.

May I read this memorandum with respect to the arrangement which has been reached. As a result of the discussion the terms of the proposal are as follows:
1.	Personnel of army, navy and air services proceeding on embarkation leave will be granted transportation at one-third of the existing reduced rates which are, round trip at the price of single fare.
2.	If embarkation does not occur within six months of the date of enlistment, personnel entitled to ordinary leave or furlough in accordance with the regulations of the three services will be granted the same reduced fare concession, that is, one-tliird of existing rates, when proceeding on such ordinary leave or furlough, provided that when embarkation leave is eventually granted to such personnel they will be entitled to such one-third fare for such leave, if the date of such embarkation leave is not less than six months after the date of such ordinary leave or furlough.
3.	Such one-third fare will apply in all other cases of ordinary leave or furlough where the date of such leave is not less than one year after the next previous embarkation leave or ordinary leave or furlough in respect of which such one-third fare has been granted.
4.	The one-third fare concession will not be available under any conditions to personnel having less than six months service except for embarkation leave.
If it should happen that a man is going overseas within even less than six months after enlistment he gets his embarkation leave on the one-third fare.
5.	Personnel granted leave or furlough under any other conditions will continue to pay existing mileage rates.
6.	The one-third fare will apply only from the location of a man's unit, ship or establishment, to his bona fide home as defined in the regulations of his own service.
I put this on record so that hon. gentlemen may see it. I think it represents a very substantia] and I hope acceptable concession to our sailors, soldiers and airmen in connection with transportation fares on leave.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and Supply):
subtopic: STATEMENTS ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
In rising to answer the questions asked by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) this morning, perhaps I should make one or two remarks about the speech of the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot). The hon. member has taken it upon himself to raise the bogy of railway amalgamation. Just why he found it necessary to mention my name in that connection and to slander a few of the officers in my department, I cannot imagine.
I occupied the positions of Minister of Railways and Minister of Transport for more than five years. I think there is nothing in my record in that office that would indicate that I had then or have had since any sinister plot for amalgamating the Canadian Pacific Railway with the Canadian National Railways, or for paying out the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific Railway from Canadian funds.
When I entered the government in 1935 I had certain business interests in this country. In order to qualify for the position I accepted, I disposed of all those business interests finally and irrevocably. Since 1935 I have had no business interests whatever in this country other than the job I have occupied as a member of the government.
My trip to England was for the purpose of carrying out certain business of the Department of Munitions and Supply. My hon. friend placed a sinister interpretation on a newspaper article which stated that I went to England for a personal reason. I do not mind telling the house what that personal reason was. It had to do with the timing of my departure on the trip. I timed my departure as I did in order to spend Christmas with my oldest boy w'ho was graduating from Naval College.
I did not meet Mr. Purvis in London. He had been there and had departed before I arrived. The fact that he had been in London had nothing to do with my trip to London. While in London I discussed the affairs of the Canadian Pacific Railway with no one whatever. The discussions I had there had nothing to do with any matter of finance pertaining to Canada. I particularly resent the slander against Mr. Purvis. Mr. Purvis, at the beginning of this war, at the request of the British government severed all connection with his business interests in Canada, retired from the presidency of the company for which he had been responsible prior to the war, went to Washington and has, I think, devoted all his working hours to the interest of the government of Great Britain. I know of no one who has had a more profound effect on the defence of Great Britain, as it is carried on in the United States, than has Mr. Arthur Purvis, and I very much regret that any hon. member of the House of Commons would gratuitously use his name as it has been used to-day. I also resent the fact that men who give their time and their service to my department should be subjected to slander in this house.
I do not know what the hon. member for Temiscouata has given up in order to serve in this war effort, but I do know something of what the men he has mentioned here have given up in order to give their time to the work of my department.
The suggestion has been made that there is something sinister in the department, and that I have bargained with the chairman of the committee on war expenditures to leave the affairs of my department alone. I may say that if anyone has a suggestion as to anything sinister in my department, the doors of the department are open for any proper investigation; but until something of a sinister nature is brought to light, I very much resent the implication that something sinister actually exists.
After all, it is part of my job to build up across Canada the thought that munitions of war are being bought honestly, efficiently and at reasonable prices. I doubt very much if any man is doing a patriotic duty who, with-
Supply-The War-Mr. Howe

out any foundation in fact or any foundation whatever upon which to base his statement, spreads the story across Canada that the buying of war munitions and the war business generally of this government are not being conducted honestly and efficiently. I make that suggestion to all hon. members in the house.
If there is reasonable evidence that that is not the situation, then I am prepared to meet any charge in that direction. I suggest, however, that those who depend upon insinuations are not performing any real service in the war effort of Canada. I apologize for having taken the time of the house to make these few remarks. I doubt if they were really called for, but as I have occasion to be on my feet for another purpose, I have taken the opportunity to make them.
This morning the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) asked for a statement as to the position of armament production. I have before me a brief statement which was prepared for another purpose, but which perhaps will place before hon. members the information desired, and I shall proceed to place it on Hansard. This summary was written for the purpose of comparing the position of Canada one year ago with the position of Canada to-day with respect to the production of armaments.
One year ago armament orders in Canada totalled less than $60,000,000. War production consisted merely of a few types of shells, together with a modest output of small arms ammunition. During the past twelve months we have built up a gigantic armament industry in Canada. Over $400,000,000 has been spent in constructing crown properties for the manufacture of shells, guns, tanks, automotive equipment, bombs and machine tools. Total war orders placed in Canada to date exceed $1,700,000,000.
To-day we are turning out Bren machine guns in great quantities; trench mortars are being turned out by a plant in one of the smaller manufacturing cities of Quebec; two types of anti-aircraft gun barrels are in substantial production, and both types of complete anti-aircraft guns will be in production by September; 500-pound aerial bombs are being manufactured and filled in our own shell-filling plant; naval anti-aircraft gun mountings, highly intricate pieces of equipment involving the manufacture of 2,000 separate parts, are in production.'To-day I can tell the house that Canada has already produced her first 25-pounder artillery gun, and this gun has passed all its firing tests. Before this month is out, these guns and carriages will be produced in considerable numbers. I can also announce for the first time
(Mr. Howe.]
that in another plant our production of 2-pounder guns has been commenced, and that the first consignment of these guns is being shipped overseas. This month has also witnessed the initial production of depth charges and mines.
A week or two ago Canada produced her first infantry tank, and this production i3 rapidly stepping up to considerable volume. Before the month is over, we shall have produced our first Canadian-made cruiser tank. It may be of interest to mention here that whereas the United States, Great Britain and Canada united to produce each its own version of a common type cruiser tank, Great Britain has already adopted the Canadian version, and the United States has asked for a sample Canadian tank for test purposes, with the likelihood that United States will also adopt the Canadian design.
Canada is now producing small arms ammunition at the rate of many hundreds of million rounds annually. We are also producing ten different calibres of shell, at the rate of millions of rounds a year. We are also producing the explosives required to fill these shells, together with cartridge cases, primers, fuses and all the shell components. Hon. members will appreciate the magnitude of the job when I state that each month we produce about 25,000,000 individual parts of shells. These shells are being produced in Canadian plants.
A new government plant has recently poured the first optical glass ever produced in Canada, and is in substantial production on optical and other instruments, and on secret radio devices. We are also manufacturing antisubmarine nets and equipment and minesweeping gear. By September we shall be in substantial production in practically every type of gun used in this war, from rifles to the largest type of anti-aircraft guns.
A year ago Canadian orders had been placed for some 9,000 automotive war vehicles, of which less than one-third had been delivered. To-day we have already delivered over 120,000 vehicles, and still have on order another 80,000 vehicles. The automotive industry is also delivering universal carriers in substantial quantity.
A year ago Canada had a small production of explosives from existing plants, and one major explosives plant was under construction. To-day nineteen plants are either in operation or nearing completion, involving a programme of $110,000,000. Ten of the nineteen plants are already in operation, and in another month the entire programme will have been practically completed. To give hon. members an idea of the physical size of this programme.

Supply-The War-Mr. Caldwell
I may say that several of our major plants each occupy an area of from one to two square miles. Our output of military explosives for this year will exceed the entire output of Canada during the period of the last great war.
A year ago our aircraft industry was turning out about two aircraft a week. To-day the industry is producing more than forty planes a week, of which about twenty are fighting craft, and the remainder, training planes. The industry is also servicing aeroplanes and engines used in the air training schools, which is in itself no small project.
A year ago Canada had converted a few smaller vessels to naval use, and ship contracts had been placed to the extent of about $50,000,000. To-day, of eighty corvettes on order, fifty-nine have been launched. Of the sixty mine-sweepers on order, twenty-four have 'been launched. Three merchant vessels have been converted into auxiliary cruisers, and twenty-seven other boats have been converted to naval needs. In addition, we are building twenty-four patrol vessels and twelve mine-sweepers of a special type. Work is under way on a cargo vessel programme, involving an expenditure of over $200,000,000. We have also in progress a substantial small boat programme. Seventeen major shipyards and forty-five smaller shipyards are occupied on this programme. The major shipyards are being substantially enlarged to accommodate the cargo vessel programme.
Our industrial expansion and other war activities have involved a very large building programme. My department has placed construction contracts involving an expenditure of over S120 million for the erection of some 3,000 buildings. More than 100 aerodromes have been constructed.
We Canadians are accustomed to think of Canadian industry as being on a small scale compared with those of Britain and the United States. We need have no inferiority complex in the matter of armament plants. To illustrate, we have in Canada the largest factory in the world producing machine guns. We have the largest plant in the English-speaking countries producing field artillery, and this is the only plant anywhere manufacturing field artillery from scrap iron to the finished product. One of our government arsenals has the highest output of small arms ammunition in the English-speaking countries. Our chemical and explosives plants are among the largest to be found anywhere. Our war production has been organized on a vast scale, but we have not overlooked the small shop. Our "bits and pieces" programme has brought work not only to the small commercial machine-shops, but to machine-shops built for
the private use of newsprint, mining and other domestic industries. We are constantly in search of new productive capacity, and if any has been overlooked, my officers would like to be advised of it.
To sum up the situation, I think we can be reasonably satisfied with our armament programme. Generally speaking, the plants have come into production as anticipated. I had thought that we would reach our production peak this summer, but as the months have gone by we have been called upon to assume additional responsibilities for new types of armaments. So far as we can see now, we shall still have an expanding programme running into the spring months of next year. I may say, however, that to-day production is up to any anticipation that I have ever had, taking the programme as a whole, and I believe that Canadian industry is capable of still further expansion. Steps are being taken to bring our output up to the new maximum that we can now visualize.

subtopic: STATEMENTS ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to say anything on the motion to go into supply, but since the ministers have been good enough to make statements regarding the questions I propounded this morning, I shall take this opportunity to bring to the attention of the government some of the reasons why those questions were asked. They were not asked to provoke the kind of statements that we have received. I did not intend to ask questions in a manner which would merely invite an answer to the - query regarding recruiting, or invite the kind of statement which the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) has just made. As a matter of fact, I think we have had too many of these statements. Statements of this type have not given to the house, and to the country through hon. members, the kind of information the country is seeking. What prompted my questions this morning was the fact that across Canada there is growing a feeling that all is not well with our own war effort. People read the newspapers, and they see the frank confessions of failure, if you will, that are made from time to time in the British House of Commons by Mr. Churchill and his colleagues. Then they pick up our own papers and read that all is going well with our own war effort. In my opinion public confidence in the government and in this house is being undermined. We are running the risk of losing that very essential thing needed to win the war- and we are going to win it-known as morale. The purpose of my questions this morning was to get a complete statement of our wai

Supply-The War-Mr. Caldwell
effort in such terms, if they could be given publicly, as would give our people a more exact understanding of Canada's effort and vital needs than they now have.
From time to time there come to me, and I am sure there come also to other hon. members, opinions as to why men are not joining the army in larger numbers or why production lags. I believe a different type of educational campaign should be used across Canada in order to keep our young men and workers filled with that idealism which is necessary to carry on a struggle of this description. That is not being given to them. In Great Britain the morale of the people has been built up; they have been convinced that this war is a struggle for something worth while, that they will not return again to the pre-war conditions of unemployment, of want, of riding the rods as we say in this country. In my opinion these things have not been stated with sufficient definiteness to imbue our own people with a similar challenge. We are remote from the bombed areas of Great Britain, and that may have something to do with the present feeling that exists across the country.
Young men who attempted to join the army in the early days of the war were told that their services were not wanted. That confirmed the opinion that there was no immediate need for the recruiting of men. Those of us who believed that Canada's part in this war ought to be the providing of munitions, supplies and other aid without profit to this land, hoped that the government would organize this country so that we would be able to plan on the basis of a maximum output of those supplies, so that we would be able to give the people an idea of what was actually required in the way of equipment and manpower. To-day many people know that the men who have been enlisted have not been equipped in a manner which would lead us to believe that we have sufficient equipment for all the men whom we have placed under arms. This interferes with recruiting.
Some men were recruited and, after being in the army for some months, were returned to civilian life on account of some physical disability. Many found themselves again in the bread-line; others found that the job they had relinquished in order to join the army had been filled by somebody else. This condition will be partly remedied by the legislation which the Minister of Labour (Mr. McLarty) announced this morning.
Then we read in the paper or hear over the air the statement that the first heavy tank has come off the assembly line. People
\Mr. Coldwell.]
are asking how many more tanks are coming off the assembly line, because there is a belief, well based or otherwise, that the production of the tank was a special effort and that we are not turning out the equipment which we ought to be turning out for our men. In fact, it is said that the tank did not come off the assembly line at all; that it was made specially for the occasion. That has been widely said across the country.
What I wanted to-day was not a general statement such as the minister has made that "production has come up to our expectations," but to ask that, either in a closed session of this house or otherwise, we should be given specific information with regard to our production of war equipment. I believe this is the only parliament within the British commonwealth which has not had a closed session in order that the government might inform the representatives of the people as to exactly what is going on. I know there is to be one in New Zealand to-morrow. That was announced over the air from Great Britain at noon to-day. I think I express the feeling which is held by many hon. members, and, I know, by the members of our own group because we have discussed it, that we as members of this house know no more of the actual position with regard to the war and our war effort than does the ordinary man in the street who reads newspaper and magazine articles regarding it. In fact, as we have not the time to read them, perhaps we know even less than the man in the street who reads these articles. Frankly I am disappointed that no arrangements have been made for a comprehensive survey of the present war position both overseas and in this country, and that this house has not been taken into the fullest confidence of the government in relation to the supply of equipment and the necessities in the way of supplies for the next few months.
We are facing, as we all know, probably the most dangerous period that our commonwealth of nations has ever faced, and yet we in this parliament of Canada have not been informed of the situation as it exists across the ocean and as it exists in our own country, or to what extent it is expected that we shall be able to provide the maximum aid possible in our war effort during the next three to six months.
The purpose of my question was not mere curiosity. I did not particularly wish to know where recruiting was slack. I asked my question in that form so that we as members might be given a comprehensive view of what was going on all across the country. Nor did I ask about production out of mere idle

Supply-The War-Mr. Coldwell
curiosity, but because I am convinced that the country feels that all is not well with our war effort and that this house should be informed so that our members may be in a position, when they go back to their constituencies, to render the greatest possible service in this dominion by assisting to maintain the morale of our Canadian people.
I said a few minutes ago to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) that in my opinion the morale of this country was not as good as it ought to be, and I am firmly convinced that one of the reasons for that is that we have not been put in a position to place before the people of Canada our war effort in the terms which they had expected.
Having said that much about the material side, let me repeat my opinion that we have not maintained the morale of our people to the fullest extent. If I may again refer to Britain, where some of us still have friends and relatives who write to us, again and again they tell us that when the war is over, a new and better England, or Britain in the larger term, will be born. The people of England are thoroughly convinced of that, and for that they are prepared to sacrifice and to fight. But we in this house have not given our Canadian people the same assurance. I said a few days ago, and I repeat, that I should like to see this House of Commons pledge itself unanimously and solemnly declare that when this war is over, every power that lies within this parliament-and all power finally rests within this parliament-will be used to ensure that every Canadian shall have the right to a job, and if he is sick or cannot find a job, shall have the right to an adequate and decent living. If we made that simple pledge in this parliament, our people would understand better what we hope for when this war is won.

subtopic: STATEMENTS ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: But instead they are preparing the people for a depression.

in this country; how many fighter planes, how many bomber planes, and so forth; and the number of every other type of war equipment that is being produced in this country. speechtext: I think my hon. friend is missing some information. Some of the information he has asked for has been given. subtopic: STATEMENTS ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes, I know.

subtopic: STATEMENTS ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I mentioned both those items, yes, but there is still a feeling in the country that the production of essential equipment ought to have been speeded up in view of the lack of it overseas at the present time. As a matter of fact, in the House of Commons in Great Britain yesterday the Right Hon. Winston Churchill appealed for greater production of equipment. He pointed out that the loss of Crete was due to the fact that we could not cover our operations there because we lacked planes and were insufficiently supplied with tanks. We may be living up to estimates which were made several months ago; we may be maintaining our schedule, but it seems to me that every effort should be made to produce in advance of that schedule. I mentioned particularly the matter of tanks because, as I have said, there is a belief, which I think is well-founded, that we are not producing heavy tanks, as many people suppose, "from the assembly line." Perhaps the Minister of Munitions and Supply can clear that up.

subtopic: STATEMENTS ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes. There seems to be a popular misconception of what is meant by "assembly line" as applied to tanks. The impression appears to be that there is a belt running down a huge factory, with parts feeding in and tanks coming off it every two minutes. Tanks cannot be built on that kind of equipment. They are tremendous affairs; I believe that each tank contains something like 2,800 separate parts. Those parts flow in from a considerable number of factories to a central assembly plant, where they are put together. Perhaps they will be placed in a line to be assembled, but certainly they



Supply-The War-Mr. Johnston
will be assembled one at a time. There is nothing of the nature of the automobile assembly line. We fully expect to turn out three tanks a day, but my hon. friend will at once realize that the process is not that of a travelling belt or anything of that sort.
The victory of getting the first tank together is that we know that the parts are complete, that they fit, and that all adjustments have been made. That is the significance of the assembling of the first tank. The others will follow more rapidly, because we can proceed with more confidence. I may add that we expect to have by the end of this month eight of that particular type of tank out of the Angus shops, and during next month we should be up to our full production.

subtopic: STATEMENTS ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is just the kind of information which I think the house should be receiving.

subtopic: STATEMENTS ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: [DOT] There are so many types of production that it is hard to cover them all. If hon. members have specific questions, I shall be glad to answer them if I can.

subtopic: STATEMENTS ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I have not seen these tanks in production. I confess, having seen belt lines in the making of other vehicles, my mental picture was exactly what the minister says it should not be: in other words, that of an assembly line. The purpose of my question this morning was to ascertain the difficulties which the government is facing in order that we may explain those difficulties to the people and assist the government in every way to maintain morale, interest and enthusiasm for what, after all, is a just cause. That, I fear, is what has not been done this session. For example, I am sure that the debate we had yesterday does not assist in that regard at all. It was a discussion of the war effort from an angle which is not informative, and may, indeed, be defeatist in its effect upon our people. I urge the government, even after these two statements have been made, to take the house, through the Prime Minister, into its confidence regarding the progress of the war, and have the ministers supplement, before we leave, what they have already told us with more specific and detailed information than we have had up to the present time.

subtopic: STATEMENTS ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Before this question is finally dropped, I wish to say a word or two. It is certainly true that we are facing a very serious crisis, and I do not believe there was ever a time in the history of the British empire when the assistance of every one was more urgently needed. One of the greatest dangers is that the people will be lulled into a false sense of security.

As the hon. member who has just resumed his seat has observed, we are giving the impression that we are doing everything humanly possible to produce all sorts of munitions and supplies, limited only by the full capacity of our ability. Personally I do not believe that impression is correct, and none of us should leave a stone unturned if it will aid in the increase of our preparations.
There is a possibility, as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) suggested, that some of us have a wrong impression about these tanks. I have never visited a plant which makes tanks; but when I heard the expression in the house that they were "coming off the assembly line", I connected it with the experience I have had of visiting automobile manufacturing plants where cars are assembled by a process which is so described. I believe that is the general conception of the term, and with that impression in mind, people build up confidence with such statements as this, "Well now, we are just pouring these tanks off, and certainly we are doing a wonderful job."

subtopic: STATEMENTS ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is what the papers have said.

speechtext: No doubt.

When one goes to the movies and sees pictures of machine-shops with everybody working at full capacity, one can understand how people get the impression that that is typical of the way in which our production is proceeding. Let me discuss for a moment a question I mentioned to the Minister of Munitions and Supply some time ago. I refer to the return for which I asked, which was passed, with reference to the Dominion Bridge company and its connection with the rolling mill in Calgary. For some time past, ever since the national war services department was started, 14873-2414
there has been a great drive to get scrap iron in the prairies for use in the manufacture of munitions and supplies of various kinds, and this question of the Calgary rolling mill was brought to the attention of the government many months ago. The
manager of the Pacific division of the Dominion Bridge company, Mr. A. S. Gentles. I quote:

speechtext:

addressed?

speechtext:
To. L. W. Killam, British Columbia committee on war production, Vancouver. This communication was tabled as part of the correspondence between the dominion government and the company. It is dated April 14. The first intimation that the company had was that an arrangement had been made for the establishment of a bar mill at Vancouver. They say:
Our company, through a subsidiary, has for a number of years successfully operated a bar mill at Selkirk, Manitoba, converting scrap and pig iron using open hearth furnaces. We also have at Calgary a similar type rolling mill which, due to economic conditions, we have not operated for some time-
This is the important part.

and which is available for immediate production at that point.

Supply-The War-Mr. Johnston
Here we are in this house declaring that we need these materials now. We started a campaign to get scrap iron, advocating that members go out and assist the organization in getting scrap iron from all the provinces for conversion into steel so that we might have immediate production. It was very urgent, the Minister of National War Services told us. If he told us that, he must have been right; I would not contradict him. But let us take his statement in conjunction with what the company says. Speaking of this mill at Calgary, the writer of the letter says, as I have quoted:
. . . and which is available for immediate production at that point.
There is no mistaking that. We could have used that scrap from the prairie provinces at the Calgary mill immediately. The whole thing was well established. The writer goes on:
In 1933, we fully investigated the economics of moving our Calgary mill to Vancouver. It is adaptable either to open hearth or electric furnace operation.
There was no difficulty in either of these because we have the electrical power at Calgary, and we also have open hearth appliances. But the government did not take advantage of that. If we needed steel we should certainly have started immediately; if we did not need steel, then the Minister of National War Services was deceiving the country. I cannot see any way out of it, and I believe the minister was quite sincere, because as the results have shown, there is an abundance of this scrap iron at Calgary. But the Minister of Munitions and Supply was going to allow this company to move their plant from Calgary to Vancouver. I do cot know whether that is still the intention or not; the Minister of Munitions and Supply could answer that question. I hope he has changed his mind in that regard. Let me quote further from the letter:
Owing to the temporary conditions created by the war and as a war measure, our company, subject to ratification by our directors, is prepared at our expense to move rolling mill equipment from Calgary to the coast, set up and operate a steel mill at or near Vancouver on the following basis.
I understood the minister to say the other day that no cost to the government would be involved. Let us see the conditions under which the mill was to be set up at the coast. First:
That the government policy in regard to scrap be such as to assure a continuous supply of steel scra,p on the coast of from 30,000 to 10,000 tons per year.
They had to guarantee that, and my information is that they can do it. About 50,000
[Mr. C. E. Johnston.!
tons of steel are already at Calgary, and I believe the estimated amount that could be collected was over 200,000 tons. There is no reason why that mill should not be operating to-day at Calgary.
The second condition was:
That the government permit the complete write-off of the new capital invested against the mill profits or the consolidated profits of our company, within a period of not more than three years, preferably two years.
The Minister of Munitions and Supply told us there was no charge to the government; true, there was no capital outlay.

has listened patiently, then certainly those of us on this side of the' house have listened to you. Now you are going to keep your seat and listen for a moment or two to us. I am not objecting to your policy. I am quite prepared to sit and listen-and at times it is pretty tough to do so-but I have the floor now.
It was not estimated that we could build 200 vessels in Canada, plus all the rest of the equipment we have been turning out. Anyone who thinks that Canada is not producing should visit the harbours of Halifax, Saint John and Montreal; there he will see the assembly of goods produced in Canada, goods which are being shipped in enormous quantities.

In matters of production we have done wonders in Canada. We have underestimated our ability to produce. I am not saying that we are doing all we can do. In what I have said I am not suggesting that we should not have a programme which would be inviting and inspiring to the people of Canada, and one which would challenge them.
I say: "Tell us what you want. Tell us the things you think we cannot do, and you will find there is engineering ability and backbone in our people, and resources sufficient to do it." I say, "If you want a bridge across the Atlantic built from boats, then tell us

Supply-Agriculture
what type boat you want, and the Canadian people will give it to you." We have a boatbuilding programme now, and it can be enlarged. Probably it cannot be enlarged in steel, because we are short of steel; but we have plenty of wood on both Atlantic and Pacific coasts, and we can turn out more wooden boats. It is not a case of whether a piece of equipment is the cheapest we can get; it is a case of what we can give to the manufacturer, and what kind of equipment we can put on the ocean to carry our stuff from Canada to England.
I do not care how proud we may be of what we have accomplished; we have lost practically the whole of the last four weeks talking nonsense in this House of Commons, instead of getting down to planning about what we actually can do.

speechtext:
I can tell you this. In my opinion it was not the budget, or the amount of taxes our people have to pay, or the war loans they have to buy, which scared the people of Canada. There is, however, something quite evident in this chamber that tells us, "You must not do this"-or that we must not do something else. There is something about us that is tightening us up so that we do not know exactly what we are supposed to do.
During the Easter recess I was talking to manufacturers in my home city, and I said this, "Streamline every bit of equipment you have. If your plant is obsolete or obsolescent, renew it and put it into a position where it will give the best service, because you will need it after the war. You need it now, and you will need it after the war." However, I came to Ottawa, and I found that if one wants to streamline his plant he must have a permit to do so. That is not a good thing. I do not think we can win this war or save this country on a stingy programme. We must go ahead. I, for one, am not prepared to sit down; I am not prepared to sit idly by. I have piled up round my own plant at the present time over $100,000 worth of equipment. My boy wrote me the other day, saying, "Dad, what do they want us to do? Do they want us to go ahead and develop our plants, make them better so that we can pay more taxes, or do they want us to quit?" That situation must be cleared up. We must
decide whether we are going to win this war by stingy methods, or whether we are going to win it by working and by production.

SO. Special. Prairie Farm Assistance Act, $500,000.
Would the minister inform the committee whether last year a crop failure area was declared in Saskatchewan?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speechtext: No. No crop failure areas were declared in any of the provinces last year.

I have before me sessional paper No. 110M, produced on motion of the hon. member for Weyburn, and dated May 15, 1941. In this document I find a telegram dated July 8 from Mr. J. G. Taggart to the minister, in the following terms:
Review of crop conditions to-day indicate heavy deterioration and certainty of more than 135 townships under five bushels. Believe it urgent to proceed with proposed amendments which I am sure will greatly improve workings of act. '
I shall not read all of the communications. There is one from the Minister of Agriculture to Mr. Taggart under date of July 31 advising that an amendment had been passed and that it would be necessary to raise the number to 171 townships. There is a further communication under date of August 1 from the minister of agriculture of Saskatchewan to the effect that the number of townships having a yield of less than five bushels to the acre would substantially exceed 171. Then there is a list of the townships, which I have not counted. But there are thirteen pages each
Supply-Agriculture

containing from thirty-five to fifty townships, and therefore the total would be well over 500. These are the townships which, in the opinion of the provincial department of agriculture, would have a yield of less than five bushels to the acre. Last night, when this matter was being discussed, the minister pointed out that where the act states that the governor in council may upon the application of the province make this mandatory, the "may" had the same effect as "shall". Would he be good enough to explain to the committee why he did not declare a crop failure area last year in view of the evidence submitted by the provincial department of agriculture at Regina?

The act requires that before the federal Department of Agriculture will even investigate to see if there is a crop failure area, the province must state that they believe there is a sufficient number of townships under five bushels to the acre to meet the requirements of the act. At the present time that figure is 171 townships; at the time the first application was made the figure was 135 townships so far as Saskatchewan was concerned. The minister of agriculture of Saskatchewan made application early in the season and declared that he believed there were more than 135 townships, all that was required at the time, and designated the municipalities which he believed were under five bushels to the acre. As is indicated by the return, I, as the minister in charge, communicated to him the fact that the required number had been increased from 135 to 171 townships. He came back with an application stating that he still believed there was a sufficient number of townships in Saskatchewan under five bushels to warrant the application being made, and he gave a list which, I assume, is the one referred to by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson). With that list in our hands we made an investigation, but this showed that there were not 171 townships which were under five bushels to the acre, and therefore we refused to declare a crop failure area.

Will the minister
explain the wide discrepancy between the opinion of the department of agriculture of Saskatchewan and that of the minister's own department?

There is not a wide discrepancy. The department of agriculture of the province does not make an investigation. All it has are the reports from the municipalities or other authorities that the crop yield is expected to be under a certain figure. We expect that they will make application for

all those townships which they have reason to believe will drop below five bushels to the acre. When that is done, we keep a check on the townships until the crop is harvested. After the crop is harvested we make a report as to whether or not the yield was five bushels to the acre. We found that there were not 171 townships in Saskatchewan with a yield of under five bushels to the acre.
How many were there?
I think the number was 156 or some such figure.

Mention was made
yesterday evening of the cost of administration. Last year I made representations to the minister that municipal authorities should be used more extensively. The minister stated that there would be difficulties, that in administering funds where the dominion had so much at stake, they could not very well give ' responsibility to the municipal authorities which naturally would be concerned about having payments made to as many people in the municipality as possible.

I was going to put on the record certain figures in connection with the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, 1940 crop year. These figures are as of May 31, 1941. The records may not be complete, but they are almost complete.. The figures are: Townships dealt with by the board

How many applications
were turned down because they had not been sent in by October 31?
I cannot give that at the moment. The number is not large in comparison with the number of application? made, but I am not in a position to give the exact figures.

The number may not be large, comparatively speaking, but the minister realizes that there were quite a number

Supply-Agriculture
turned down on account of that fact. Many applications were late because the municipalities believed that the yield would be above twelve bushels to the acre, but upon the completion of threshing operations it was found that the yield was below twelve bushels to the acre. Will the minister object to a certain action that I am taking? I am writing to all the municipalities in my constituency reminding them of what happened in 1940 and suggesting that they make application before September 15, should it appear that the average yield is going to be less than twenty bushels. Apparently last year they tried to estimate whether the yield in the township would be less than twelve bushels, and many of them fell into the error of overestimating the yield. This is the action that should be taken if Ottawa is going to stand by the hard and fast rule of refusing to accept applications because they are sent in too late. A farmer in a municipality should not be discriminated against because the municipality has tried1 to do the right thing. I think the minister will appreciate what I am talking about.

The desire of the department is that the provinces and municipalities notify the federal authorities of any township which they believe will, on the average, go under twelve bushels to the acre. We have also intimated to the ministers of agriculture in the provinces-this probably was not done in sufficient time to take care of last year's crop-that we would much prefer them to err on the side of asking for those townships which we might turn down upon investigation to their erring on the other side. Any western member, indeed any hon. member of the house, will realize that it is difficult in the early part of July to say just what the crop yield may turn out to be, but we have been hopeful that some authority will notify us fairly early in July as to what they believe the crop yields will be in those townships. I think the government of Saskatchewan have probably been more active in that connection than governments of other provinces, probably . because they have had more costly experience; for there have been much larger drought areas in Saskatchewan than anywhere else, and they have probably a more complete organization to check conditions all over the province. For these reasons perhaps they have put in more applications and got them in at an earlier date.
There was a difficulty, I must admit, in Alberta last year in view of the change through the death of the provincial minister of agriculture who was carrying on in the early part of the season, but we did intimate finally to them that we preferred that they
would err rather on the side of indicating to us that a township should be examined which might not come within the area upon investigation to their erring on the other side. There were not very many townships that were passed over, if we are to judge by the number that came in afterwards and said that they had not been aware of the fact that they were under twelve bushels to the acre until after November 1. I have the figures here of those that were examined in the different provinces and will add them to the figures I have placed on the record in order to give hon. members some idea of the number of applications made in the different provinces.
In Manitoba we examined 316, and we passed 171; in Saskatchewan we examined 2,126, and we passed 1,271; in Alberta we examined 431, and we passed 224. It will be noted that there is not any great difference in the proportion of those passed, compared with the number examined in the three provinces. In all three provinces we examined 2,873, and we passed 1,666. I am informed that the number which have written in later from all three provinces and questioned whether they should not have been in, stating that they had not made application because they did not have information sufficiently early or for some other reason, is considerably less than 100. Therefore, out of over 2,873, it would be a comparatively small number. Applications were made in the case of these 2,873 before November 1, and they were all examined. I realize, of course, that that does not help the people who were in those districts which found they were under twelve bushels to the acre, and they have reason to complain that someone did not take action in sufficient time. I must say, too, that we do not absolutely rely on these applications that are sent in. Our inspectors do check some of the townships when they are in areas where they realize that a township may be making application later on. They will check some of these townships which have not asked for it, but we do not feel that we are expected to act unless a municipality or a province makes application.

But after the inspector finds out that the yield in such a district is below twelve bushels, does he not notify them to make application, or does he wait for them to find out? I think it is up to the inspector to tell the municipality that the district will be eligible for the bonus, without waiting to see whether they make application.

The inspector is not in a position to give anyone definite information. He checks a certain proportion of the farms
Supply-Agriculture

in the district and gives his opinion that a certain township may come in, to the officials in the office, not to the municipality. There is somewhat of a check kept. We always expect that the municipalities will keep a check.

To return to the question of personnel, I have done a good deal of business with the department in Ottawa and with the office in Regina, and I think the minister is fortunate in having such an efficient personnel at headquarters. I am sorry I cannot say the same of the personnel in the country. Looking over the list of inspectors operating in my constituency, given in the return brought down for the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley), I have been struck by the expense accounts of some of the inspectors. This is the first year the act has affected the northern part of Saskatchewan where I live. I should like the minister to state, first of all, how the personnel in the country is selected. I notice the name of John Davies, for instance, of Farmingdale. How does the minister find out that John Davies, living away up in the bush, is a suitable person for this work?
Second, I should like to know what sort of check the department makes of the expense accounts of these inspectors. The hon. member for Lake Centre pointed out last night that one inspector working out of Melville turned in an expense account averaging $11.50 a day, and looking over the list of inspectors and their expense accounts I find a wide discrepancy. In my constituency most of the inspectors run up an expense account of nearly $10 a day. The cost of living is not as high there as in other parts of the province, and I notice that some other expense accounts are for $5 a day, and that some inspectors draw less for expense accounts than in salary. A great many are paid $5 a day in salary and run an expense account of around $10 a day. In my constituency I stayed with a friend at a hotel at Easter time. We had supper, bed and breakfast, and in the morning I asked for the bill and was told they were charging us two dollars. I asked, "Two dollars each?" and they said "No, for the two." True enough, the hotel was not in the style of the Chateau Laurier, but it was the best and only hotel in the village, and I cannot understand how these inspectors doing their work in the field can run up such large expense accounts. Would the minister tell the committee how these men are selected, and what check is made on their expense accounts?
In selecting the men, we try to find some one who is not looking for a permanent job.
There are plenty of them in the country.

Yes, but I think there are more who are looking for permanent jobs. Generally we try to find someone, to put it in another way, who is not in absolute need of a permanent job, who has some other employment. If we can find a good capable farmer who has had considerable experience and is in a position to give us probably two or three months of his time during the summer, and if he thinks it will not interfere too greatly with his own farming operations, we like to have a man of that type. Or we might choose a man in a village who has been accustomed to dealing with farmers, either through being in some branch of the grain trade perhaps or through making collections, and who knows farm lands and can estimate crop yields when he sees them, even as standing crops; he understands farming operations, and at the same time is prepared to devote to the work part of his time during the summer. We make some inquiries to assure ourselves fairly well that the man has either a business or a farm to return. That is the type we hope to get. We do not wish to call men away for anywhere from two to three weeks or two to three months, and have them say to us afterwards, "We expect you to find work for us for the remainder of the year."
This is one check we do apply. We make inquiries of municipal men, of members, of persons here and there over western Canada in order to find suitable types. For example, the first man who was put on, I believe, is one of the best-known municipal secretaries in Saskatchewan, a man who is known by every municipal official in the west; I refer to Mr. Truseott. I understand that he attends all the municipal conventions, and has done so for many years. He was given the task of going over the block of country of which he has charge at present, and selecting half a dozen men to go out immediately as' inspectors. He made recommendations, and the names were placed on the list. In most districts we have asked for at least double the number of men whom we expect to use, and we leave it with the officers at Regina to select men from that list. They use a man for a period of time. If they find that he is efficient in the work they continue to employ him, and probably they will call him up the succeeding year. If they find that the man does not do the job as they wish to have it done, he will probably not

Supply-Agriculture
be called up the next year; they will try someone else. But the lists are made up in the manner I have explained, and they are submitted to me as minister for my endorsa-tion. Some of these men I know; many more I do not know, and I simply have to take the word of those of whom we inquire, who know these men, as to their abilities, and try them out.
The other question was what?
About their expense accounts.

The expense account, naturally, is made up of their board and sleeping accommodations while they are away from their homes, and the cost of operating their cars. A car operates on a basis of seven cents a mile until 4,000 miles have been covered, when it becomes six cents a mile. The cost in connection with the car is made up from that calculation.
As to how some of them might run up large expense accounts, that depends upon the type of work a man is put on. If a man is put out in a district the greater part of which is in a crop failure area or in which the crop is obviously under twelve bushels to the acre, he does not need to make the number of inspections which have to be made by a man who is working in the borderline areas. For example, a man can drive rapidly through a township which has three bushels to the acre, and say, "That is under five bushels" or "under four," as the case may be. But he cannot drive nearly so rapidly through a district which is on the boundary line between eight bushels and seven, or eight and nine, or twelve and thirteen, or twelve and eleven. The man who operates for the greater part of his time in the area of which I first spoke can earn much more on mileage, because he would cover probably double the area, entailing double the expense in mileage, and consequently might build up a large expense account. Burglund is one of the main checking men who has made inspections and checked areas which have been gone over. He is one of the men in the district who are sent out to check areas, and in many instances to recheck areas.

The hon. member for
Mackenzie has, I think, touched a vital point. I had some experience last year and the year before in our district with these men. I talked with them, and found that the man who was inspecting the municipality in 1939 was driving home to Windthorst, about forty miles, every night and running up his expense
account. I may say that he was checked up on this, and then he stayed in about the centre of the municipality.
I brought this matter up yesterday, and I contended that men who had a knowledge of the municipality should be reemployed if they are doing good service. In the instance I have in mind, a change was made last year. Another man, who, as the minister states, is a farmer in the district, did this work, and while I believe he was conscientious in many respects, he made what I would term a still quiet hunt. He inspected every quarter-section, driving round quietly, and put in an expense account considerably greater than his salary, and I would venture to say that nine nights out of ten he was at his home. I have here the list to which the hon. member has referred, and it shows that at least 70 per cent of these men have expense accounts which run over their salaries.
Twice as much.

Yes; some of them twice as much. I venture to say that the minister could make a great saving if these men were checked up in that respect. If the same man continued to do the work this year in that municipality, he could complete it in one-fourth of the time, because he has knowledge now of every quarter-section and of every farmer. In consequence, his expense account would be materially less.
As regards this matter of individual inspections to which the minister referred, the system followed last year amounted practically to individual inspection of every farmer and every farm in the areas to be inspected where they thought that the crop was such that the producers would come under the bonus.
I am not going to hold up this matter any further, other than to say this, that it is under this act, and under this branch, I understand, that the minister is to carry out the regulations with respect to the reduction in wheat acreage, the summer-fallow bonus, and so forth, this year.
Yes.

How many additions does the minister expect to make to the staff to do that work this summer? What increase has there been in the staff in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, with respect to this particular branch of the work?
The minister will recall that in 1939 there were quite a number of overpayments of bonus, and I believe he took steps to recover some of those payments. What success has he had in that direction? I have in mind four or five cases; I am not going to mention
Supply-Agriculture

names, but I think the minister knows some of them. I know he was undertaking to make recoveries, and if there have been overpayments there should be some method of obtaining repayment. I believe also that there are a number of cases yet unsettled, still more or less in dispute, with respect to last year. How many are there, and what does the minister propose to do? Will there be some settlement of these cases?

There are about one-third of the questionable payments-I would not say it has been definitely decided that all of these questioned payments should not have been made-that have been collected. About two-thirds of those in respect of whom payments were questioned have not yet paid back the amounts. We have not been so much concerned about persons who were actually on farms and received overpayments or received payments when we afterwards found out that probably the land should not have been paid for on account of some of the regulations we have. Knowing the districts particularly in areas that have been on a number of occasions in the drought zone, we figure that if that farmer is due a payment later on we can withhold the amount out of succeeding amounts to be paid him. We have not been so persistent in pursuing these persons. There are some difficulties in compelling the repayment of moneys where persons have turned out not to be farmers, but all doubtful cases have been turned over to the Department of Justice, and they have been examining into these cases and trying to determine those that may be in a classification under which action can be taken. Up to date, however, no actions have been taken in court to collect. The result is that we have collected one-third of the money which we think should be repaid.
To give an idea of the amount which is involved-because a general discussion of this kind could leave the impression that with the payment of between $9,000,000 and 810,000,000 in the first year there might be a considerable part of that money about which there was some question-I might point out that the total amount questioned by the treasury department and ourselves is $13,156.73, and the recovery has been $4,736.22. In paying out a sum of money that is considerably over $9,000,000, under a plan that is entirely new, over such a wide area, and to some 58,000 people, we were fortunate not to have more cases than we actually had, and we are also fortunate to have been able to collect back about one-third of the amount. Most of the persons who returned the payments sent back

the money quite voluntarily as soon as they found they had received payments to which they were not entitled.

How much was collected from the farmers for the last fiscal year, and what is the amount of payments made under the act in the same period? I wish to refer to a letter from the secretary of the United Farmers of Saskatchewan dated March 25, 1941. Copies went to the various political parties from Saskatchewan, and no doubt the minister has seen the letter. I promised that I would try to get an explanation, because there have been certain complaints about the board of review. I quote:
I am enclosing a copy of an appeal which we have presented to the board of review, under the chairmanship of Professor E. C. Hope of the Saskatchewan university. Here we find a rather strange situation, in that I first of all presented the first two cases referred to in the appeal to A. R. Maekie, superintendent in charge of administration of the act. He refused the bonus because of a "ruling of the treasury board in December, 1940". I then referred these two cases to Hon. J. G. Gardiner, Minister of Agriculture, and he replied that he could not change the ruling.
They cite some nine or ten cases that came before the board of review. Could the minister make a short statement in connection with these problems to which attention has been directed by the United Farmers of Saskatchewan?
First, I would ask the minister to be good enough to give an answer to the question I asked. What was the increase in staff to carry out the regulations with regard to summer-fallowing?

I have not the exact
figure here, but I understand that the increase in inside staffs will be about a dozen in the three provinces.
How about the field staffs?

There has been no
increase in staff in the areas in which we were operating and the more southerly areas where there have been crop failures or low crop yields, but we have had to add to staffs in the northern sections, through the northern part of Manitoba, the. northern part of Saskatchewan and into the northern part of Alberta, and we have had to make appointments in the Peace River section of British Columbia. The numbers on the outside staff will not make any material difference. The persons added on are added to the lists I have indicated. People are selected from these lists to do the work, and if double the number are selected they will do it in half the time,

Supply-Agriculture
so that the figures in that regard are not as important as the total amount of money paid out in doing the work.

I understand that there
were quite a number of men who went lecturing and attending farmers' meetings.

Very few of these men
were employed. The provincial departments of agriculture offered the services of all their district agricultural men, and they went and held meetings. Many of the municipal secretaries, although we were paying them only for office work, held meetings in different divisions of their municipalities voluntarily, and they are paid on the basis of fifty cents a farmer who applies for a reduction in acreage, for all the work they do throughout the area in connection with the applications. They did make it convenient for farmers by holding public meetings and having the farmers come to the schoolhouse, or wherever the meeting was held, and sign their applications for wheat acreage reduction, but nothing was paid for these particular meetings.
What about those cases still in dispute, not yet settled? The minister knows the ones to which I refer.

I understand there are about a dozen individual cases before the board still for consideration, and there are a number of townships or applications from individuals that are before the Department of Justice for decision as to whether they are entitled to payment.
Will this be the final regulation with respect to the summer-fallow bonus and acreage reduction?

It will be final unless there are unforeseen developments. An undertaking was given here regarding a matter about which certain questions have been asked a number of times by hon. members in the last two or three days. I believe I am correct in saying that an undertaking was given by the Minister of Justice and myself that in order to make provision with regard to the right of members to apply, if it becomes necessary to do so, an amendment can be made to the regulations. Amendments of different kinds may have to be made, but in substance the regulations are as we intend them to operate.
The answer to the other question is this. In 1939 the number of townships was 1,923; payments, $9,904,300.77, and the levy $2,421,507.37. For 1940, to date, the number of townships is 1,666-this figure is a little larger than the one I put on record because it is of a later date. The payments amount
to $6,500,217.18, and the levy-we have not the exact figure-is approximately $2,500,000, or almost identical with that of last year. It was $2,421,000 last year, and it will be in that neighbourhood now.

475.	Special. To provide for assistance to encourage the improvement of cheese and cheese factories-further amount required, $395,000.
Will the minister break this down, the amount for equipment and the amount for cheese?	.
