Mr. Chairman, when we were discussing this item some weeks ago, the minister made a statement in connection with the sale of the salmon pack of British Columbia. He stated at that time what had been done up to date. Since then, I believe there have been some further negotiations in the matter. Prrhaps he would be willing to make a further statement.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. E. MICHAUD (Minister of Fisheries):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall be pleased to comply with the request of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni and make a statement supplementary to that I made on May 26. Additional information has come to my attention since, and I shall inform the committee as to the further developments in connection with the matter of supplying the canned salmon requirements of Great Britain.
Last week the British food controller stated definitely that he was desirous of purchasing the canned salmon pack of the British Columbia fisheries for the present year. Immediately the Department of External Affairs, the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of Fisheries set machinery in motion not only to give the assurance that this request would be met, but to give an undertaking that everything possible would be done to get together those large quantities of fish required to supply British needs, and to see that shipments were properly coordinated and shipped overseas in an orderly fashion.
Will the Canadian government buy the fish direct from the British Columbia people?

No. We believe the industry on the Pacific coast will take care of those requirements, as it has done in the past. We have advised the British food controller, through the British mission, that a maximum pack of 1,700,000 cases of salmon could be properly put up this year, if our expectations are realized, without impairing the future of the industry. Not only have we said that we would do everything possible to see that it was put up and delivered, but we have pointed out that home requirements and a certain share to go to other markets would be taken care of. We have assured the British government that we expect the industry to deliver 1,200,000 cases of canned salmon this year to the British market and, in order to make that possible, we shall have to curtail by 40 per cent the usual quota for home consumption and for markets other than British, or reduce the amount to 60 per cent of that packed for export to markets other than British and for home consumption.
This means that we shall keep about 500,000 cases for our requirements in Canada and for export markets other than those in Great Britain, and that we shall make available to the British consumer 1,200,000 cases.
How does that compare with last year's catch?

To give the committee an idea of the magnitude of the undertaking, may I point out that the average export to

Supply-Fisheries
Great Britain in 1936, 1937 and 1938 amounted to 380,493 eases of canned salmon, while last year's shipments amounted to 568,441 cases. It is obvious, therefore, that our commitments this year are about double last year's shipments.
It is estimated that the pack mentioned by the minister as 1,700,000 cases can be produced this year. How does that compare with the amount produced last year?
It is between 350,000 and 400,000 cases more than the production of last year. In order to assure these British requirements, we shall have to take every precaution to see that priority is given.

Priority will be given to the
British orders?

Yes. Members of the
committee may be interested in knowing the basis of this sale of salmon to Great Britain. The pack is divided into three grades: grade No. 1, comprised of sockeye; grade No. 2, comprised of cohoe and red spring, and grade No. 3, comprised of pinks and chums. The prices are to be from 10 to 15 per cent higher than those received last year, to take care of the additional cost of production. The prices for this year are $13.75 a case for No. 1; $10 for No. 2 and $6.25 for No. 3; the prices last year were $12.37 for No. 1; $8.65 for No. 2 and $5.60 for No. 3. These prices are for a case of 96 half-pound flats.

Is there any indication that
these prices, apparently set by the British government, will be satisfactory to the fishermen and the canneries?

So far as I have been
able to ascertain, they will be satisfactory to the canneries, and I have no reason to believe that they will not be satisfactory to the fishermen. The fishermen must consider themselves fortunate in having an assured market this year for this large quantity of fish, with conditions as they are. Had the British government not consented to take this large quantity, I doubt if the home market and the markets other than British would have been able to absorb such a large quantity. Since this year's prices take into consideration the increased cost of production, I think the fishermen ought to be satisfied with these prices.

This seems to be an excellent arrangement provided that the required quantity can be obtained. Unless this happens to be a big run year, it will be rather difficult to get this quantity. However, the canneries will have an assured market, which they had not last year. The same condition will apply to
the fishermen. I think the government ought to be congratulated for whatever part they took in bringing about such an arrangement.
The statement was put out to the press a few days ago by the department in connection with canned herring. I understand that the British government have agreed to take 35,000 long tons of canned herring, whereas last year they did not take more than 8,000 or 12,000 tons. This is an increase of over four times, a tremendous increase.
I hope it will be found possible to supply this quantity, but I doubt it. This bears out the argument which I have been advancing for many years and which I mentioned last week, that the Canadian government ought to stop the reduction of herring into oil and other products. It might be easy for me to say, "I told you so." For all these years I have been telling the government that they should not permit the reduction of herrings into comparatively low-class articles like oil and fertilizer. In that way we get the least possible out of the fish; we curtail spawning, and we reduce the amount of salmon food which is most essential. When a crisis comes along and there is an enormous demand at a profitable price for herring, we find that we shall not be able to supply anything like the quantity required.
We have out-fished these herring in years gone by, and enormous quantities have been reduced. The departmental reports show that the supply has been steadily going down. There is one step the minister could take, a step which he has the power to take, namely, to prohibit any reduction of herrings this year. It may be said that the more profitable price to be received for canned herring will bring about this result, but that does not necessarily follow. A plant may be equipped for reducing only, and it will go on reducing only, first pilchards and then herring, if allowed to do so. Great Britain does not want herring in the reduced form because she can obtain what oil she requires from whales, cod, et cetera, but she does want herring in this form. Apparently it is intended to have these put up in half-pound tins in order that they may be part of the men's rations, part of what they call the special ration. The minister should fall in line with the expressed wishes and needs of the British government. This will be to the advantage of the fishermen and canners because more money can be obtained from a ton of canned herring than from a ton of reduced herring.

The British food controller has expressed a desire to be supplied with a large quantity of canned herring this year. As a matter of fact, I think it is the first
Supply-Fisheries

time in the history of the British Columbia fisheries that canned herring has been demanded in such a large quantity. Thirty-five thousand long tons is what they ask to 'be supplied with. This will mean 1,630,000 cases of ninety-six half-pound cans to the case. In this connection, priority will be given to meeting these requirements. I am inclined to believe that when they are taken care of, there will be little left for reduction purposes.
Without committing myself definitely to a policy of prohibiting altogether the reduction of herring this year, I can assure the hon. gentleman that so far as I know, reduction will have to be prohibited in many sections. There is always a certain quantity of fish caught which are not suitable for canning or any other purpose than reduction for fish meal. There are fish caught which cannot pass the inspection and cannot properly be put into cans and offered to the consumer. Nor can they be thrown back into the water and be wasted, and we shall have to see that they are used to the best advantage and supplied possibly to other interests, particularly agriculture, for use as food rations for poultry, cattle and so forth. I think I am safe in saying that unless we have an overabundant supply of herring this year, we shall have to stop the reduction of herring at least until the requirements of Great Britain are assured.
Thank you.
The minister promised on May 26 to give a breakdown of the expenditure on lobster control.

I am pleased to give the hon. member the information which he requested, and which I hope will correct the misapprehension under which he was labouring on a former occasion, on May 5, when we discussed the [DOT] expenditures for the canned lobster industry.
The season for canning lobsters opens generally in May. Last winter, after the government of Great Britain had placed canned lobster on the luxury list, the fishermen as well as the canners thought they could not operate with a market as limited as the Canadian and United States markets, judging from the volume of former exports. They appealed to the government, and we had to give them the assurance that the usual pack would be taken care of and that we would help to market it. The average annual pack of canned lobster for 1934, 1935, 1936, 1937, 1938 and 1939 amounted to 97,000 cases. Last year we amended the regulations and prohibited the canning of lobster smaller than six and a half inches in length. We knew that that would tend to reduce the pack and

also to conserve the species. We also knew that a number of people who formerly gained their livelihood through lobster fishing had become engaged in other employment which they thought more profitable, and that the number of lobster fishermen would, therefore, be much smaller. It was, in fact, much smaller, but we anticipated a pack of 70,000 cases, and we gave our undertaking to the fishermen and the canners that we would see that this pack would be marketed.
We referred the matter, based on these figures, to the different boards advising the government as to production and marketing, and we adopted a plan which we thought would be helpful. We had no alternative but to try to develop the United States market and the home market. The consumption in the domestic market up to last year had amounted to 3,000 cases annually, and our average annual exports to the United States were around 12,000 cases, making a total of about 15,000 cases consumed on this side of the Atlantic ocean. The rest of the pack was exported mainly to Great Britain and some to the continent, where France, Germany and Sweden were the most important markets.
In order to influence the Canadian consumer to give some consideration to this commodity, we adopted the plan of advertising the goods on a wide scale, bringing to the attention of Canadian housewives the advantages of using canned lobster to a greater degree. Second, we canvassed the most likely purchasers in the United States, the large distributors of foodstuffs through large chain stores. The department, in order to give every assurance possible to the industry, decided that we would purchase whatever the industry itself could not sell. In other words, we agreed to be in the market to take up the slack. The results of the advertising were beyond our expectations. It is true that last year the pack was much smaller than we anticipated due to the factors I have mentioned and also to the fact that the weather last fall was much against lobster fishing, on account of several storms that raged on the coast during the fishing season in which many lobster fishing traps were carried away and much time was lost during the height of the fishing season. The actual pack was 58,898 cases. The department was offered 10,000 cases by the packers, who could not find a market for it themselves. These offerings were subject to inspection, and we could not place our seal of approval on some of the offerings. We refused to grade 4,757 cases, and we marketed 5,365 cases for the industry. The rest were marketed by the industry itself and by those who have been

Supply-Fisheries
for some years in the brokerage business and have made it their business to market this commodity.
Who were the brokers?

The brokers on government sales? We had no brokers. We sold through the controller. The deputy minister had been appointed as controller under this scheme. He employed Mr. Akins of Toronto, who consented to act without pay and who received only $1,300 approximately for expenses.
But he belonged to an advertising firm in Toronto, did he not?
Yes.
Then his commission would be got on the advertising?
I do not know what he would get on the advertising. The firm was paid $50,000 to carry on the advertising campaign we had mapped out.
Well, then, the firm would get about 15 per cent of that, would it not?
I do not know, because we do not pay the commission to the advertising firm.
They get that from the magazines?
They get that through the newspapers or publications which carry on that work.
Well, then, it was really paid through the advertising from the firm?

Yes. Accordingly we
spent $50,000 on advertising, and the cost of marketing was $12,471.22. We had prepared for marketing 30,000 cases. At the opening of the season we had undertaken to take care of 55,000 cases, and we started to establish a structure and get the machinery to take care of that amount. After the spring season was over, we found that the quantity would not be as large as we anticipated, and we reduced our set-up considerably. We had labels and cases on hand to take care of about 30,000 cases.
The price per 8-ounce can was pegged at twenty-seven cents, was it not?

No. That price represented an agreement among the retailers of the fish; it was not the price set by our
department. The average price at which we sold was, on the Canadian market, $16.15 per case; on the United States market, including exchange, $19.40. Those are wholesale prices. The retailers agreed among themselves as to the retail price.

How many cans are in a
case?

Ninety-six half-pound
cans.
There are only two months in which lobsters are harvested. What do these control men do during the rest of the year?
The controllers?
Yes. Are they kept on pay?

No; they are not
employed by us during the rest of the year. Two persons were employed in Halifax by the salt fish board, and during the lobster season we engaged them-an accountant and a bookkeeper-to keep track of the goods. We had nobody employed during the year except during the time that we took to gather the surplus which was offered to us and dispose of it.
The minister said, when he rose first, that I was under a misapprehension on May 5. I do not think my mind is at all changed yet.
Yes. From a reading of a statement of the hon. member, I gathered that he seemed to be under the impression that all the money we spent, $62,471.22, was expended in marketing 5,365 cases.
No; 4,410 fths cases.

At the time those were the figures, yes. But I am now giving the statement for the whole year, the final figures having been revised by the treasury. The controllers sold 5,365 cases; the cost was $12,471.22; but we had a set-up at the beginning of the year to take care of 55,000 cases; we had a warehouse in Charlottetown, one in New Brunswick, and one in Nova Scotia. When we found out what would be required of us, we closed two of them and kept open the one in Halifax, assembled all the merchandise there, and disposed of it from the one warehouse.

Mr. Chairman, during this discussion of the administration of fisheries, I wish to review the federal-provincial relations with respect to the Fisheries of Quebec. Though long discussed, the question has not yet been definitely settled. However as I shall show further on, it is almost settled
Supply-Fisheries

in reality. Indeed, there remains practically only to give the form of a permanent agreement to. what has already to all intents and purposes become an accomplished fact. There can therefore be no better occasion to bring the question to the fore, in the hope that both governments will this time arrive at a definitive settlement. Certain aspects of the matter lie beyond the scope of those of us who are neither lawyers nor experts in constitutional law. I shall therefore approach the matter solely from the point of view of the development of the fisheries of Quebec and particularly of the improvement of the fisherman's lot, which after all are the main things. Following a brief review of the discussions, I shall look into the bill paid by the fishing industry and the fishermen of Quebec and the basis of the permanent settlement advocated.
The question is far from new. It has its roots in the confederation pact itself. Confederation laid the foundations of a dispute between the dominion government and the various provincial governments. This dispute is still going on, at least in so far as Quebec is concerned. Taking its stand on the subsection "fisheries" of the British North America Act, the dominion government assumed both jurisdiction and ownership in respect of fisheries, not only deep-sea but also inland, save as regards small rivers and lakes. The dominion government, therefore, issued the licences, permits, leases, etc., for both commercial and game fishing. The provinces soon took the matter to the courts. The first litigation concerned inland fishing and the first province to institute proceedings was New Brunswick. As far back as 1883, in the then famous case of Robertson vs. the Queen, the Supreme Court of Canada invalidated the lease granted by the dominion government on the Miramichi river, thus recognizing the provinces' property rights in their territorial waters.
Following this judgment, the province of Quebec began immediately to exercise the prerogatives proceeding from the recognition of its property rights. Ottawa, however, did not renounce its judicial power and, consequently, its legislative power, which, in any case, no one had ever contested. It continued and still continues to make laws and regulations respecting the conservation of fish in the St. Lawrence and our other rivers and our lakes. In the interests of harmony, Quebec has supplied and paid, though in no way obliged to do so, the personnel required for the effective administration of these laws and1 regulations.
In 1898 the provinces challenged the dominion's jurisdiction over fisheries in tidal

waters. The case, that of Quebec and Nova Scotia against the dominion, was heard by the privy council. In his judgment, Lord Herchell rejected the dominion's claim by establishing clearly the fundamental difference between legislative control and property right and affirming that one did not necessarily derive from the other. In 1914 the case was resubmitted to the privy council, this time by British Columbia, and again in 1921 by Quebec alone on account of the special situation in which it found itself in that regard. In the judgment which ensued, Lord Haldane held that the province, as a result of its ownership of the land, was entitled to ownership of any fishing gear attached to the land in any manner whatever, not only in the river estuaries, but anywhere along the coast. Our province was therefore entitled* to issue permits and licences. But, as the right to fish in tidal waters is a public right, Lord Haldane denied to the province the right to issue exclusive leases or fishing rights therein.
Its rights having thus been clearly established and defined as regards its deep-sea fisheries, the province of Quebec set about exercising them by requiring, from 1921 on, a licence for salmon-fishing and for fishing-gear attached to the land along its coast.
But as the dominion government enjoyed, for purposes of legislative control as well as of revenue, the same right, though to a lesser extent because it did not in its case proceed from the right of ownership, it likewise required a licence. Our fishermen thus found themselves obliged to pay two licence fees. Furthermore, a fisherman holding a provincial licence but unable to obtain a federal one for the same purpose, or vice versa could only fish at the risk of breaking either a provincial or a federal law.
Such a situation could not last. Out of it arose an agreement with respect to our deep sea fisheries, along the lines of the one that had been concluded some thirty years before in connection with our inland fisheries. The dominion authorities retained the legislative power previously vested in them, as I said, and Quebec undertook to supply the staff required for the administration of those federal acts and regulations.
An agreement like that of 1922 could only effect a temporary settlement. Its full operation, with the inference drawn therefrom, could not and did not satisfy our province.
Consequently, as early as 1931, that is eight years after the agreement, a movement was launched in Quebec with a view to bringing once again that matter to the attention of the public. An editorial published in Le Soleil on March 24, 1931, stated the case.

In February 1932, the legislative assembly passed a resolution to the effect "That it was expedient that dominion-provincial cooperation be effected so that the development of our fisheries might be better ensured." That resolution found an echo in the House of Commons where all members recognized the benefit that our fishermen would derive from the cooperation of the two governments.
The question having thus been raised, the papers in turn took a hand in it. A delegation requested his Lordship Bishop Ross of Gaspe to lead the movement. He agreed on two conditions the wisdom of which cannot but be commended: (a) The matter should be considered solely from a social standpoint, outside all party considerations; (b) the newspaper campaign should cease. With his customary sense of duty, Bishop Ross set out upon his task. He met with the best reception on all sides. However, he wanted a complete agreement, with a complete programme. Honourable Messrs. Duranleau and Laferte had an interview and as a result the fisheries station of Grand River came into being. That was something, but it was merely one item on the programme. Consequently, in a letter to I'Action Catholique which that paper published with his permission, in its issue of April 18, 1933, the worthy bishop of Gaspe expressed his disappointment and authorized that paper to take up once again the campaign it had formerly waged so vigorously.
In 1934, the matter of cooperation between the dominion and the province with respect to fisheries was raised again in the Quebec legislative assembly by the then member for Gaspe, Mr. Alexandre Chouinard. Among those who took part in the debate were Mr. Pierre-Emile Cote, member for Bonaventure and now Minister of Lands and Forests, and Mr. Edgar Rochette, member foT Charlevoix-Saguenay, now Minister of Fisheries.
The late hon. Mr. Kelly, who had raised the question in the legislative council, took it up again in 1935 and a substantial extract from his speech can be found in the February 28, 1935, issue of 1 'Action Catholique. That was the end of it.
That the agreement of 1922 entailed a great loss for the Quebec fisheries and indirectly for the fishermen is now generally recognized. Let us consider these two points, among others: industrial development and federal grants.
The war of 1914-18 greatly depressed the fisheries of Canada and, as ever, the dominion government, being so vitally concerned, launched a reform and expansion plan. The fillet industry along with the salt and smoked fish industry took a great expansion. Great strides were made in the use of fish waste and
Supply-Fisheries
inedible fish, and in the matter of cold storage. The maritime provinces benefited from all that. The dominion government helped in every possible manner that expansion of fisheries along industrial lines, and in order that the fishermen from the maritime provinces might benefit from it, they even organized a fleet of fish-collecting boats.
Let me clear up one point right now, Mr. Chairman. In contrasting our position with that of the maritime provinces, we are not prompted by envy or jealousy, and our hon. friends who represent that part of the country in this house should not take offence. We have a respectful admiration for them. When they want something from the dominion government, they ask it with such strong and persuasive arguments that they never fail to succeed. Our task would be all the easier if we could prevail upon them to teach us their methods.
The best standard for ascertaining the development of the fishing industries is the marketing of fillets, a modern product in great demand among housewives. These fillets are sold fresh, frozen or smoked. Here are the figures for Nova Scotia and Quebec, according to official statistics:

However, I must say that during these last few years the fillet industry has progressed enormously in Gaspe. But, until 1938 Quebec had had no share in that development. Until the depression, the situation was not very bad because the dried cod market had quickly improved and become quite good between 1922 and 1929. However, the depression would have been less severe in 1932 if, as early as 1921, we had organized our production so as to secure our share of the national market. Since the depression, our fisheries have hardly regained 10-7 per cent of the lost ground, while Nova Scotia registered a gain of 45 per cent. And the reason is. that the dominion government have not dealt with Quebec as they should have done. The whole industry has suffered from that arrangement. The bill has been paid by the fishermen. And from the amount paid in direct relief by both governments since 1932, one can see that the bill was pretty stiff. What makes it all the more distressing is the fact that, in 1921, the dominion was to begin in earnest to develop the Quebec fisheries.
Supply-Fisheries

In 1921, the dominion was ready to develop the Quebec fisheries according to a plan, which was set aside as a result of the 1922 agreement. That plan included the four following items: (a) building up of a competent technical staff; (b) higher salaries, in order that the members of this staff might devote their entire time to their duties; (c) establishment of a divisional fishery office at Quebec; (d) setting up in the Gaspe peninsula of an educational centre destined to become a combined biological and experimental station.
It should not be forgotten that Quebec's contribution to the national income is almost one-quarter of the total. It is only fair, therefore, that Quebec should obtain from the fishery appropriations a share somewhat proportionate to its contribution to the national treasury, or at least according to the number of its fishermen. Such has not been the case. Even before the agreement of 1922, Quebec did not receive its share; far from it. Take, for instance, the years 1904 and 1914, in connection with administration and fish-culture :

More figures could be given, but these should suffice. Our fisheries and our fishermen are still feeling the effects of this parsimonious policy. In 1906, when our lobster-banks were being overfished, the Gaspe peninsula had only one inspector of fisheries, whose territory comprised the entire lower St. Lawrence right up to and including the county of Bellechasse.

The same year Cape Breton alone, in Nova Scotia, had 27 inspectors. To-day, as everyone knows, our lobster fisheries are petering out. The average intake per lobster-trap has diminished from 66 pounds in 1890 to 8-2 pounds in 1932.
While prior to the agreement the province of Quebec received far less than its rightful share of the appropriation, its situation in that respect became much worse afterward. All grants, all contributions to administration costs ceased. Would it be possible to estimate Quebec's loss on that score? Doubtless the exact figures could be arrived at by setting down for each year either our contribution to the national income or the evolution in the number of our fishermen. That would be a long and unnecessary task, as the ratio would probably be the same as for the two years given above-1904 and 1914. The federal fishery appropriation for the twelve years following the agreement has averaged $2,000,000 a year. On the basis of our contribution to the total national income our rightful share would have amounted to $500,000 a year, or $6,000,000 for the full period. On the basis of the number of our fishermen we should have been entitled to something between $2,500,000 and $3,000,000. Wre received practically nothing, on the ground that the administration of the fisheries was a provincial matter.
To this amount must be added what Quebec had to pay directly for the administration of its fisheries and the development of fish-culture, some $150,000 a year, which in the other provinces is paid by the dominion government, and rightly so. While administra-

Supply-Fisheries
tion expenses are necessary, the fisherman cares little whether they are paid by Quebec or by Ottawa. But what he does care about is that Quebec, the provincial government which has done the most for its fishermen, is forced to divert to the administration of laws which Ottawa continues to make an amount of $40,000 to $60,000 a year which could be usefully employed directly for the development of fisheries and the improvement of the lot of the fishermen. If the dominion had, from the first decade, sought to make compensation by devoting an equivalent amount to the assistance of the fisheries of Quebec, the balance would have been restored and the question solved.
As far as fish-culture is concerned, the dominion government assumes the costs in the other eastern provinces and allows the provincial governments to draw the revenues, by means of licences and leases, derived from its restocking of their rivers and lakes. The fact of Quebec having the administration of its deep-sea fisheries in no way frees the dominion government from this responsibility.
What connection is there, indeed, between the administration of deep-sea fisheries and the artificial breeding of rainbow trout and speckled trout for the restocking of lakes and rivers? Yet, the dominion government assumes responsibility for the latter in the other provinces.
Therefore, to the above mentioned losses, must be added the sums appropriated for the administration of fisheries and pisciculture, and of which the development of the fisheries of Quebec has been deprived.
The fishermen and the fisheries of the province of Quebec have thus been fleeced. However, I do not wish to blame anybody in particular. I just wish to expose the facts in an impartial manner and assist in correcting a condition that nobody wanted, I am sure.
Could our fishermen be thus legally despoiled through the agreement of 1922? I am not competent to appreciate fully the juridical effects of that agreement, but if the federal government admits its obligation to help improving the condition of the fishermen, the contribution must be the same everywhere, and it is unjust to favour one section while discriminating against another. In my opinion, as members of the Canadian community, our fishermen can not be left out of the distribution and if they have been deprived of their natural rights by the agreement of 1922, it is through a biased interpretation unforeseen by its authors. In a democratic country, the government has no right thus to despoil an entire class of the population
of one province. Jurisprudence, if I may use that word, agrees with my assertion. To extend the help that the present Minister of Fisheries has given to our fishermen during the last few years-for which I express my sincere gratitude, on behalf of all the fishermen of the Gaspe peninsula-it has not been necessary to rescind the agreement of 1922.
As a matter of fact, the two governments have done good work. During the first decade, that is from 1922 to 1932, the progress was rather slow; in Ottawa, because of the wrong interpretation given to the agreement, and in Quebec, as a result of a lack of organization inherent in such a succession. During that period, the province of Quebec, nevertheless, did some fish-culture, organized cooperation among fishermen, helped the cold storage industry, started to train specialists, established her administrative service, promoted the classisfication of fish and encouraged through grants the building and outfitting of fishing boats. During the last eight years Quebec has increased and diversified her aid, and covered the coasts with a wonderful network of cold storage plants. She has taken the leadership in endeavouring to gain for her fishermen a place on the national fish market, and she has promoted hydrobiologic research and established a fisheries school.
During the same period, the dominion has discarded its former policy. It has established an experimental fishery station in the Gaspe peninsula. It has paid grants to indigent fishermen, extended to our province the benefit of the salt fish board and, last but not least, it has contributed to the development of education among our fishermen. Thus cooperation between the two governments is not only possible but is actually taking place.

Thus, a definite and final agreement is but the logical result of the work now being done; it will be the means of dealing with many matters that are not yet settled. Among the numerous tasks that devolve upon governmental authorities, there are some over which the dominion alone has jurisdiction and executive power; others might properly be assumed by Quebec and, finally, there are many where joint action, if carried on properly, might be twice as productive.
Among the tasks about which the dominion cannot delegate its powers to the provinces,
Supply-Fisheries

may be mentioned sea patrolling and market protection. Both have an international character and it is difficult to see how the provinces could act efficiently in that respect. To those tasks could be indirectly added the classification of products. In the field of deep sea fisheries, the province of Quebec has dealt alone with that. But with respect to export products especially, would not a national classification impress importers more than a provincial one?
The proper function of the province of Quebec is to obtain a place on the national market, to promote production and to develop new industries. Finally, the two governments can actually cooperate, though not equally, in bringing about the general expansion of markets, in the development of scientific methods and their application to industry, in the extension of educational facilities and in the organization of cooperative societies. An agreement in that common field would have the advantage of preventing a duplication which, though non-existent at this time, is nevertheless, possible.
To those activities might be added fish culture. In our province and in British Columbia, the provincial authorities assume complete responsibility for it. However, cooperation by the federal government would be welcome and easily justified. In our province, in spite of the two administrative agreements concluded, the federal government has kept absolute jurisdiction over all our species of fish, without exception. I think that this should naturally entail the duty of restocking our waters. That is the case for the eastern maritime provinces and the local governments are even allowed to derive revenues from fishing licences and leases in the waters restocked at great cost through the federal government's own fish hatcheries. Quebec would be satisfied with less. Our province is doing a considerable amount of work in that field each year, but the size of the job offers plenty of opportunity for federal cooperation.
Quebec and Ottawa are fully cooperating in the development of our natural resources, especially mines and agriculture. The two governments have definite agreements in relation to youth training, unemployment, old-age pensions. Why not in regard to maritime fisheries? A few improvements in the present conditions, as I have just suggested, the defining of each one's part in the fields where the two governments cooperate, and everything would be definitely settled. In my humble opinion, it is time to give a character of permanence to this tacit but too fragile agreement, which is, however, essential to the success of the work undertaken.

I am under the impression that the agreement concluded between Ottawa and Quebec in relation to the fisheries is not complete. In order to get rid of us, the officials at Ottawa appear always ready to answer that Quebec has entire jurisdiction over her fisheries and that she has to look after their needs.
What about our share of subsidies, Mr. Chairman? We pay our share of taxes to the federal government, far more than the three maritime provinces combined. It is true that this government, as I said before and as the Minister of Fisheries explained the other day, has done more for the fisheries of Quebec than the Conservative party ever did. However, I maintain that during the war the estimates of the Department of Fisheries should not be reduced. I am convinced that the fishermen will suffer from this reduction in the estimates. The fishing industry is a national industry, just as much as agriculture, and it is during the war that we should try to obtain the best returns from it.
Mr. Chairman, I must add that I have full confidence in the present Minister of Fisheries and in the government of the Hon. Mr. God-bout at Quebec. I sincerely hope that the two governments may conclude a permanent agreement through which the province of Quebec shall obtain her legitimate share of grants.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to call to the attention of the committee an injustice, which has been done certain residents in the counties of York, Carleton and Victoria in New Brunswick, whose lands front on the non-tidal waters of the Saint John river, by reason of an order in council passed on May 9, 1940, and now embodied in section .9 of the special fishing regulations affecting that province. The effect of this so-called regulation is to take away from those people rights in property which legally belong to them, without any compensation whatsoever.
To take away from a man what he owns, without his permission and without compensation, is a theft, and I charge the Minister of Fisheries and the government of this country with the theft of property, by reason of this order in council. I realize, in saying this, that I am using rather harsh language, but I use it deliberately. I charge the Minister of Fisheries and members of the government with the theft of property, and I believe the only defence they can offer is that when they passed this order in council they did not realize what they were doing. That defence,

Supply-Fisheries
after all, is a very poor excuse. It does not justify their action, and it does not correct the wrong that has been done.
The regulation in question reads as follows:
The use of nets in non-tidal waters, except under a permit from the Minister of Fisheries, is prohibited.
That sounds innocent enough; but owing to the fact that no permits are ever granted, its effect is, as I have already stated, to deprive these people of their legal rights in property, without any compensation whatsoever.
In order that the committee may understand the position, I shall refer to it in some detail. At the conclusion of the revolutionary war-

In order that members of the committee may understand the effect of these regulations, it is necessary for me to explain the situation. At the conclusion of the war of the revolution the United States government passed edicts of banishment against the person and acts of confiscation against the property of those men who had been loyal to and who had fought for their king during that war. In consequence, these men, their wives and their children, who were known as united empire loyalists, were obliged to leave comfortable homes and a well-established form of living, go to the British colonies in the northern part of the continent and there, amidst great trials, hew out for themselves new homes in the wilderness. About 70,000 persons left the United States at that time and laid the foundation for a great nation in the northern part of this continent.
Some of these loyalists settled along the banks of the Saint John river in the province of New Brunswick. As a reward for their services they received grants of land from the crown. These grants conveyed not only a certain acreage of land, but, if the description of the Saint John river as given by the Minister of Fisheries on August 3 last, as reported at page 2449 of Hansard, that the waters in the summertime are very shallow and narrow, is correct, then there is no doubt that these grants extended to the centre of the stream, and that the owner of the soil was the owner of the fishery above it. There can be no question about that. I might add in passing that if the Minister of Fisheries intended by that remark to convey the idea that the river was non-navigable, I am in agreement with him. I agree with him that the river is shallow in many places, but I must take issue with him when he says that the river is narrow. I cannot give its average width, but in many places it is over a thousand feet wide.
The important point, however, is that the grants to these loyalists conveyed not only a certain area of land, but also, and I quote from one of the grants:
All . . . fishings, fishing waters . . . profits, commodities, appurtenances and hereditaments whatsoever thereunto belonging or in anywise appertaining.	*
Now grants of this kind convey what is known in law as several fisheries, and in the case of these grants they convey a corporeal hereditament. They gave the exclusive right
Supply-Fisheries

of fishing to the grantees, their heirs and assigns in the waters fronting on their land to the middle thread of the river, or, as some text books say, ad medium filum aquae. If the Minister of Fisheries has any doubt about this statement, I would refer him to Hals-bury's "Laws of England," second edition, volume 15, commencing at page 42.
The most important fish that frequent the Saint John river is the salmon. There is only one way in which that fish can be caught in these several fisheries, namely, by netting. They will not rise to a fly; they will not take bait, and they cannot be caught by trolling. In consequence, from the time these grants were given about the year 1785 until last year these loyalists and their successors in title have exercised their legal right to net these fish in their several fisheries. It is hardly necessary for me to point out to this committee that netting is one of the best known and one of the oldest methods of catching fish. It was probably an old method when Simon and his brother Andrew cast their net in the sea of Galilee. It is the only way in which salmon can be caught in these several fisheries and, in consequence, the effect of this so-called regulation is to prohibit the owners of these several fisheries from exercising their rights to catch these fish in their several fisheries in the only way in which they can be caught. It takes away their rights and property; it amounts to a theft of property. It is a wrong which cannot be allowed to go unchallenged. It is an act of injustice which must sooner or later, and the sooner the better, be corrected.
The statement made in this house by the Minister of Fisheries on August 5 last, when he said, as reported at page 2454 of Hansard:
It is possible for them-
That is, the riparian owners.
-to catch by angling if they want to use that method.
-was, I regret to say, misleading and incorrect. As I have said already, these owners cannot catch these fish by angling. In all the 120 odd miles of the fiver in question, there are only four or five pools in which salmon can be caught by angling. I ask the minister to keep in mind the fact that these pools are not publicly owned. They are owned by private individuals; and if they are fished by the public-and I believe they are- it is only with the permission of the owners.
For several years prior to last year the government has required the owners of these several fisheries to take out fishing licences before they put out their nets. When this matter was before the committee last year the Minister of Fisheries stated that these

owners had never claimed that their rights had been encroached upon by their being compelled to take out these licences. In making that statement the Minister of Fisheries showed a lack of knowledge of the law. There is no question, that the government has the right to impose a licence under the British North America Act. Under that act the dominion government has .the right also to make regulations for the conservation of fish. The regulations provided that the nets used in this river should be thirty fathoms, or 180 feet in length. The practice had been for an owner to place stakes on his land and on his land under the water for a distance of from thirty to fifty feet out into the stream. The net was hung from these stakes, and then from the last stake the net was carried down river. Since the river in many places was a thousand feet wide, a net extending into it for fifty or sixty feet did not prevent the salmon from finding their way up the stream to the spawning grounds.
There is no doubt that the government has the right to make regulations. But it is one thing to regulate, and it is another thing to prohibit. It is one thing to make regulations as to how a person shall use his property, but it is an entirely different thing to say that he shall not use that property at all. The right to regulate implies the continued existence of that which is to be regulated-in this case, fishing in these several fisheries. But a prohibition takes away a right that previously existed. The effect of this regulation is not to regulate at all, but to take away absolutely this legal right in property, and that is why I have referred, as I have gone along, to this regulation as a so-called regulation. It is not a regulation at all. It is an absolute prohibition.
By orders in council passed on February 23, 1894, and February 23, 1895, the dominion government submitted to the Supreme Court of Canada a number of questions for the purpose of setting at rest differences of opinion which had arisen between the dominion government and the provincial governments regarding rivers, harbours, lakes and fisheries under the British North America Act. The riparian owners, I might say in passing, were not parties to this litigation. The case is reported in 26, Supreme Court of Canada Reports, at page 444.
The Supreme Court of Canada answered some of the questions submitted to it adversely to the dominion government, and some questions adversely to the provincial governments, and, in consequence, both parties appealed to the privy council. The privy council held that section 91 of the British

Supply-Fisheries
North America Aot gave the dominion government the right to make fishery regulations, and that the provincial governments had no jurisdiction to make such regulations, but it pointed out that the aot did not convey to the dominion government any proprietary rights in relation to fisheries but gave it certain legislative jurisdiction. The privy council in the course of its judgment said:
It must be remembered that the power to legislate in relation to fisheries does necessarily to a certain extent enable the legislature so empowered to effect proprietary rights.
The words "to a certain extent" in this sentence cannot be overlooked. They are of the greatest importance. It was never expected nor was it ever intended that the power to make regulations would be exercised so as to deprive citizens of this country of what legally belonged to them.
During the course of the presentation of their case before the privy council, it was submitted on behalf of the provinces that if the power to make regulations was vested in the dominion government, the power might be abused so as to amount to a practical confiscation of property.
Dealing with this argument the privy council said:
The suggestion that the power might be abused so as to amount to a practical confiscation of the property does not warrant the imposition by the courts of any limit upon the absolute power of legislation conferred. The supreme legislative power in relation to any subject matter is always capable of abuse but it is not to be assumed that it will be improperly used; if it is, the only remedy is to appeal to those by whom the legislation is enacted.
The fear expressed by the provinces when the case was before the privy council that this power if placed in the hands of the dominion government might be abused so as to amount to a practical confiscation of property has now been realized. Section 9 of these regulations has the effect of practically confiscating private property without any compensation whatsoever. It is an abuse of legislative power which must be abhorrent to any court of British justice and to all British subjects.
The questions which the privy council was asked to answer in this case had to do with differences that arose between the dominion and the provinces over their respective powers and their respective jurisdictions under the British North America Act. But there was another question which the privy council was asked. It was asked as to the rights of the riparian owners. These riparian owners were not before the court to present their case and, 14873-242
in consequence, the court refused to pass on their rights without hearing them. The privy council said:
Their lordships must decline to answer the last question submitted as to the rights of riparian proprietors. These proprietors are not parties to this litigation or represented before their lordships, and accordingly their lordships do not think it proper, when determining the respective rights and jurisdictions of the dominion and provincial legislatures, to express an opinion upon the extent of the rights possessed by riparian proprietors.
It might be noted in passing that these judges observed a fundamental principle of British justice, namely, that when a man's rights are in question he has a right to be heard before judgment is passed. Their grasp of fundamental principles of British justice is in marked contrast to the manner in which the Minister of Fisheries dealt with these people when without hearing them, he passed a so-called regulation confiscating their property.
When I brought this matter to the attention of the house in August last and pointed out the injustice that had been done to these people, the owners of these several fisheries on the non-tidal waters of the Saint John river, the Minister of Fisheries at once rushed to the defence of this so-called regulation. I was surprised that he adopted this unjudicial attitude in view of the fact that a fundamental principle of British justice was involved. I was more surprised at the arguments he presented to this committee. He said that the regulation merely restricted a right; that all it did was to control the method of fishing; that these riparian proprietors had simply been regulated as to the method of exercising a right; that "We have not interfered at all with their right to fish, if they had a right"; he did not think the department had dealt unjustly with these people.
I take issue with him on the statements he made. This so-called regulation does not restrict a right; it is an absolute prohibition; it is not a control of fishing, but is an absolute confiscation of private property. These people have been treated like non-Aryans living under a nazi regime.
That is an indictment!

I do not wish to become too personal about these matters. There were some things I was going to say which, perhaps, I might just as well omit. But I will say this. It is only natural that, if you prohibit absolutely the catching of fish in certain parts of a river, more fish will be caught in other parts of that river. It is only natural that if you stop all netting, all catching of fish, and allow all the fish to reach their spawning

Supply-Fisheries

grounds, more fish will be propagated. If the government of this country considers it advisable, either in the interests of wealthy anglers and their friends and supporters, or in the interests of commercial fishermen in other parts of the river, to take away from people in the non-tidal waters of the Saint John river their legal rights, to deprive them of their several fisheries, then I tell him that there is a right way and a wrong way to go about this matter. The wrong way is the method he has adopted by having this so-called regulation put into force. The right method is to expropriate the property owned by these people and to pay them what it is worth.
When private salmon clubs like the Resti-gouche or the Bonaventure wanted to improve the fishing in their river, they did not run to the government and ask it to take away somebody else's property in order that their sport should be benefited; they went to the fishermen along those streams and at the mouth of the rivers and paid them for their stands, and then they removed those stands. They acted in an absolutely legal and proper way.
I do not think there is any hon. member in this chamber who wants to see a person's property taken from him or stolen from him. But this so-called regulation has had that effect; it has taken away from these people their legal rights and property, and it has made no provision whatsoever to pay them for their rights.
The Minister of Fisheries said in August last that at some time-he did not say when- they were going to compensate these people to the extent of paying them for their boats and nets. That, as I said then, was but adding insult to injury. That is but a minor part of their claim. Their claim is based on a legal right of property. They are the owners of these several fisheries, and you cannot deprive them of their property by order in council followed by a special or any other kind of regulation.
The wrong done to these people must be righted. I regret that in the dying hours of this part of the session, I have been obliged to take up the time of this committee in discussing this matter. But I make no apology for doing so. A wrong has been done to these people. It is a wrong that must be righted, and the sooner it is righted the better.

I do not rise to discuss this matter. I merely desire to say that the hon. member for St. John-Albert has done a great service to the people

living along the Saint John river by bringing this matter so fully to the attention of the committee.
As to the legal position, I do not think there is the slightest doubt. I do not say that a property right has been taken away explicitly, but the effect of the order in council has been to take away a right which riparian owners have had since the days it was first granted. Under the constitution of the United States that would be absolutely illegal and unconstitutional; compensation would have to be made. Under our position the crown need not make compensation, but surely there is an ethical principle which should appeal to the minister. If it is the desire of the government and of the department that, there shall be no further netting in the non-tidal waters of the Saint John river, thus taking away a right which has been enjoyed for nearly a -hundred and fifty years, the only decent thing to do, and one which should have been initiated as soon as the order in council was passed, is to ascertain what the rights are worth and pay the riparian owners. It would not be a very large sum, and it would be to the credit of the minister if he would at once institute proceedings to have this done.
From the point of view of politics this is a cardinal mistake on the part of the minister. I do not know of anything better that he could have done for me in my riding than just what he has done. Make no mistake about that; this is a vote-getter for me and against the government, and also in the constituency of Victoria-Carleton. That, of course, is not a proper principle upon which this matter should be discussed. I congratulate the hon. member for St. John-Albert upon his study of the legal aspects of the matter. I appeal to the minister to have the legal position investigated if he has not already done so, and do justice to these owners.
One word on the question of lobsters. I regret that I was not in my place when the item was discussed a moment ago, but I was busy composing a cable to my former leader, and it was, I wish to assure the committee, a labour of love. I suggest to the minister that his handling of the lobster pack last year was an ilustration of how government cannot transact private business. What happened? You had a lobster pack on your hands, and an extraordinary sum of money was spent to sell this lobster pack, 5,320 cases. In a return brought down to the house, No. 131, on November 25 of last year, on the motion of the hon. member for Cumberland, we find that a total of 5,320 cases were sold up to October 31, 1940, and that the sum of 883,139 was paid, not to the fishermen, but to the canners; that the cost of operations in

Supply-Fisheries
the marketing, handling and storage of the processed lobsters during the year 1940 at Halifax, Shediac, Charlottetown, and another place, was: for services, $6,733; for expenses, $2,602; making a total of $9,335, plus a sum of $538 for rental, plus $36,571 for cost of additional expenditures itemized, including $30,948 for advertising. The total expenditures, apart from the amount paid to the canners, was $46,446; the amount paid to the canners was $83,139; the total amount of the expenditure was $129,585. The actual amount received by the fishermen themselves, I venture to suggest, was less than one-third of the whole. Take away the cost, including the sum of $30,000 for advertising, take away the sum of $83,000 paid to the canners, and I suggest that not more than $40,000 of this money went to the fishermen. I am sure that half of this was paid out in the operations of the canners.
It may have been the intention of the department to help the canners, but I do not think parliament voted the money for that purpose. Parliament voted the money, if I apprehend the situation correctly, to help the fishermen and not the canners. What has been the result? Out of a total expenditure of some $130,000, I venture to suggest that less than one-third has gone to the fishermen. That is not good enough. Some other method must be adopted to deal with this industry. I suggested not long ago that the canning of small sized lobsters should be discouraged as far as possible. Anything under nine inches should be prohibited, and the propagation of the live lobster should be encouraged. It is the one method of dealing with the situation, even if the season has to be extended.
This situation arose in 1932-a short season, small lobsters. The government of the day handled it in a little better fashion. I admit that the canned lobster pack question was not to the front then. What we did in 1932 was to limit the size of lobsters that could be taken out of the water, and anything smaller than nine inches had to go back. We also extended the season for the fishermen, and the results to them were most satisfactory. Their income was more than doubled, especially in the fall. That is the only profitable method of handling the lobster fisheries. We must propagate the live lobster industry, putting the small lobsters back into the water so that they may grow and come to maturity. I suggest that, with the lobster considered such a delicacy as it is not only in our own market but in the markets of the United States, many more dollars would accrue to the primary producer than under the canned lobster industry.
In my opinion the whole situation must be reviewed, and I ask the minister to review it.

Certainly the country is shocked to think that it cost this much money to sell 5,320 cases of lobster-$45,000. It is ridiculous. I do not care who is the father of this scheme; it is ridiculous. It is uneconomic; it is unsound- I cannot find adjectives strong enough to condemn it

and if the minister does not change it, he will hear further from me in succeeding years.
I know there is trouble in dealing with the situation. There is difficulty in connection with export. There is an absolute prohibition in effect so far as the other side is concerned. There is trouble in getting the product into the United States-just why, I really do not appreciate, unless it is competition with their own production. At any rate, the only solution for the lobster fishery

and I am thinking of the fishermen and not of the canners-is to propagate the live lobster industry. By c_ doing, I suggest that the lobster fisherman would get $5 for every $1 he now ^ets with his catch going to the canners.
The minister ought to look into this matter. I do not know what he is doing 'this year, but I presume he is following the course he did last year. I have not made inquiries. But if he does follow that course, and if he indulges in the costly advertising he did last year, he will hear from the daily newspapers of the country. If one wants to advertise an article of food, does anyone think that he should! go to a high-class magazine in Canada, or to the daily newspapers where people see the advertisements? Fifteen per cent of .the total amount is paid in commissions to some advertising agency in the city of Toronto. What is the connection between the advertising agency and the gentleman in Toronto who drew the $1,000 for expenses and -took no salary? Is he the advertising agent? Does the minister know? I am not going to say more about that, but I should like to have an answer to that question: What is the connection between Mr. Akins, or whatever his name is, and the advertising agency? Are they one and the same person? Will the minister review the whole position?
I suggest that the minister should do everything he can to encourage the live lobster industry and to foster exports to the central provinces and the United States where the product will find- a good buying .market, rather than to encourage further canning of this delicacy. In so doing, he will preserve the industry. If you continue taking seven-inch lobsters, how long will there be lobsters? It is suicide; it is not conservation at all. I visualize the time when there will be no lobsters if we do not do something about the matter, and we ought to do it in conjunction with the United States on the Atlantic coast.
Supply-Fisheries
Propagate this wonderful sea food, preserve it, and above all, pursue that course which will bring most in dollars and cents to the primary producers.

Just one word. There is a word I do not understand in the remarks of the leader of the opposition. I have followed him closely for the last five minutes, but I think he made a slip. He is familiar with all the intricacies of the English language, but he said something that astounded me. He spoke of lobsters, a subject which is dear to his heart and which is appreciated 'by all those who are fortunate enough to eat lobster. Of course, the lobster will live; it will live long enough to be caught when it is the right size, and lobsters should not be induced to commit suicide, as the hon. gentleman has said. If the lobsters are committing suicide; if they are killing themselves, how can he 'blame the minister for that? The hon. gentleman should be more careful about his use of the English language. To-day he said that I had made a savage attack; that is another feather in my cap. But when he speaks of lobsters, would he be kind enough to explain to the committee how lobsters are committing suicide? Did he ever assist at one of these hara-kiris of lobsters? Is it done at the time they see the red bait when they are in the trap, or when they are still alive, ready to be broiled? The hon. gentleman must know. It must be one of the secrets of the Tory party.
Why make a joke of it?

The leader of the opposition made a joke of himself by using improperly the English language, a man who occupies the seat where that great philologist Arthur Meighen and that great viscount Lord Bennett of I don't know what sat. Let him explain what he meant by that.
Do not be ridiculous. You have been ridiculous all day.
The hon. gentleman is ridiculous himself.

speechtext: The item before the committee is for the administration of the Department of Fisheries. It is out of order to discuss questions of grammar or vocabulary.

I regret that I cannot undertake to try to revise the great lobster industry on the principles laid down by the leader of the opposition. This committee knows well the reasons why the government was compelled to intervene in this industry. As I have already stated, it was because those interested, both fishermen and canners or

manufacturers, were fearful that they would have to close and abandon that otherwise profitable industry in view of the fact that the market of Great Britain and other European countries was closed last year by reason of the war. Up to last year, 85 per cent of the annual pack of lobsters was sold on the European market; about 5 per cent went to Canada and 10 per cent to the United States market. Last year we were faced with this situation, that twenty thousand people, depending practically on that industry on the Atlantic coast for their cash crop, were to lose it. The only cash that most of them draw out of the fishing industry is from their lobster catch, which lasts six weeks of the year in each district. Now it is being stated that, owing to the policy adopted last year by the department, the fishermen suffered. Here are the facts. First I must tell the committee that it takes two hundred pounds of live lobsters to make a case of canned lobster, or, in other words, two hundred pounds of raw material to -make a case which contains forty-eight pounds of canned lobster. Up to last year the fishermen were receiving for their raw material from three cents to four cents a pound. When we adopted this scheme last year and agreed to help the marketing of the catch, we made it a condition that the packers should pay the fishermen at least five and a half cents a pound for their raw material. Those who would offer their product to us and seek the help of our organization to dispose of it had to produce a certificate from the fishermen that the raw material cost them five and a half cents a pound. That is the first benefit derived by the fishermen.
This year we have again given this assurance to the trade, because last year was not a normal year. Had it been a normal year, with the success we had in marketing the pack, the government would not have intervened this year; but in view of the fact that it was an exceptionally low year, the trade was fearful that with a normal pack they could not take care of it. Again, a large number of people who depend on this industry for their livelihood would have been thrown out of employment, and we would have had to make it up by relief.
Does the minister speak of those employed by the canneries?
No, the fishermen. The fishermen do not can their fish.

I know that. Do not tell me that. Why could these lobsters not be shipped to the live lobster market just as the other lobsters?

Supply-Fisheries
Because there is a limit to the fresh lobster market. Anyone who knows anything about it should know that.
The great market of 130,000,000 people that I have heard about for the last thirty or forty years cannot absorb the lobster catch of Prince Edward Island? That is nonsense.

There are sections in Prince Edward Island, the Magdalen islands, the northern part of New Brunswick from which it would not be feasible to market live lobsters on the Montreal, Toronto or United States market. Fishermen from those districts cannot profitably market their live lobsters in the United States in competition with lobsters from Maine.
Why?

On account of the distance, the cost and the climate. Because of the lower temperature of the water, lobsters do not grow as large in those sections as they grow in Maine. For that reason, if the lobster is not canned, it cannot be marketed profitably. That has been established by all those who have some knowledge of that branoh of the industry. If it were more profitable for these fishermen to sell their lobsters alive rather than in cans, with the added cost of the work, the waste and the capital that goes into the plant, and cans and boxes and labels, they would do so. But it is a physical impossibility.
There are too many fresh lobsters now on the market. .
If they fed them all in in one day.

We have created a demand on the United States and Canadian markets for canned lobster such that to-day in some sections accessible to the United States market they find it more profitable to can their large lobsters and sell on that market, which is very high at the present time.
The hon. gentleman says that we spent 862,000 to market five thousand cases. That is wrong. We spent that money to help market the whole pack, which was 58,898 cases.
Then the minister's return is wrong. I have a return certified by the deputy minister showing the total number of cases was 5,320 plus forty-five.

It all depends upon what question the hon. member for Cumberland asked. The whole pack put up by the industry last year was 58,898 cases, and our endeavour
was to help the industry to market that pack. We would rather not have marketed any, had the industry been willing to market it all. But they came to us and told us that they were fearful, and had had no experience in the domestic and United States markets. The most which had been marketed on the Canadian and United States markets in the past had been 15,000 cases. They were expecting to put up 70,000 cases, and they actually put up 58,898 cases. They asked us to help them to market the product. They suggested, and we all agreed to confer. We got them into a conference before the opening of the season, and it was agreed that the best way to proceed was to create a demand on the home market.
The minister knows nobody wants canned lobster if he can get fresh lobster.

Yes, but how many can afford to buy fresh lobster? In the winter time it cannot be purchased. It is available only during a restricted period of the year, and the cost of keeping fresh live lobster is tremendous. People in Toronto and Montreal are the largest customers. It would be scarcely physically possible; and even if it were possible, the price of taking the commodity to those markets, and keeping it there in a fresh condition, live, all the year round, would be so great that the cost could not be absorbed.

Of course it could not be handled in that way. It could not be kept on the fish market, but it could be kept by those to whom the producers sell. That is so, because I have seen it done. It can be fed into the market in the early months of the year, and in the fall.
Yes; but that is a limited and restricted market. It is a de luxe product.
Quite so.

We proved last year that this is a commodity which a great number of people will take, when they are educated to it. We succeeded in educating them. I shall give the committee an indication of what I mean. Last year on the Canadian market we sold 28.000 cases, while in the past we had marketed only 3,000 a year. We marketed on the United States market 30,366 cases, while in the past we had marketed only 12,000 cases.
All right, carried.
Now-

Carried.

-about advertising, we had figured on a production, last year, of 70,000 cases. We could not spend more than $50,000. We thought it was reasonable, based on the possible production of 70,000 cases.
It does not look reasonable now, does it?

Yes, it does. It was not intended to be a yearly appropriation. It was intended only for last year and, as I said before, had production last year been normal we would have discontinued it. The industry, with the cooperation of the government, has proved that the whole pack can be marketed, both in the United States and in Canada.
It was an innovation, to meet an emergency.
Oh, the reserves are called up.
The criticism which has been lodged by the leader of the opposition is about the only criticism we had had so far with regard to this matter.
Then the minister has not read the daily newspapers.

The daily newspapers are not criticizing. Some have asked for explanations. I am coming to that. My hon. friend knows the value of advertising. In the past, when we had a sum sufficient to spread it across the country, we did spread it among all the publications in Canada. There are 961 daily and weekly newspapers we could use. Had $50,000 been distributed among 961 publications, no single publisher would have received a great deal. We have thought that lobster can best be advertised, with only a limited amount of money at our disposal, by using coloured advertisements. We use coloured advertising exclusively, for two reasons: We think it is the most appropriate way of advertising lobsters; second, we were restricted in the amount of money we had to spend, and we thought that in view of the small amount we had, this would be the best means to get our product before the public. The result from last year's experience has proven that method to be satisfactory.
The hon. member has asked for information regarding the gentleman who carried on the advertising. I do not know his relationship with the Walsh advertising agency, except that he has had advertising experience. He holds himself out as the Toronto agent of the Walsh advertising organization, the head office of which is at Windsor, Ontario. Advertising is always placed on the same basis, namely,

on a space basis. Payment is made on a tariff rate arranged among the publications in Canada, including the daily and weekly newspapers and magazines. That tariff is known and published. It is checked by the treasury, and they all charge the same rate. We have nothing to do about it; we cannot change it. The publications control those rates, and we must submit to them.
Carried.

Pardon me; with regard to the Saint John river I would make one or two observations. I have no doubt that the hon. member for St. John-Albert was not serious when he accused me of theft. He has since given me a certificate of honesty, and I am satisfied. I suggest, however, that he was not altogether fair, nor was the leader of the opposition, when they based their whole argument on the fact that we were depriving these good people of a vested right. It was not our intention to do so, and I am sure we did not deprive them of the vested right of fishing.
Prior to last year that portion of the Saint John river above tide-water was the only nontidal water in which salmon was netted. In all other provinces and in all other waters the netting of salmon was not permitted. The action has been taken for the purpose of conservation. This controversy has extended for many years. The leader of the opposition knows that when he was a minister representations were made-
We resisted them.

Yes, I know. But the hon. member was in a difficult position. Several of those people, availing themselves of the opportunity of taking out licences for the netting of salmon, were residents of his constituency, and also voters. I do not blame him for resisting the representations made, and for not implementing those recommendations.
But we have not deprived these people of their rights. Regulations have been enforced against these people which provide that they shall not fish after dark; that they shall not fish in months other than those between May and August; that they shall not fish with certain kinds of flies. There have been many restrictions. There were restrictions on those who did not avail themselves of the privilege of taking out a licence. We have now told them-

The minister has been referring to regulations. The

Supply-Fisheries
department is legally entitled to regulate, but it is not entitled to pass a regulation which has the effect of confiscation or prohibition.
Hear, hear.
There is a legal distinction.
We did not confiscate. We simply said, "You shall not use your right-"
Without permission.
"-without permission, if you wish to use a set net."
But the minister will not issue a permit. That is the effect.

We say, "If you wish to avail yourself of your right to take that fish with a hook and bait, or with flies, there are no restrictions whatsoever." It has been said that these fish do not rise to a fly. Well, statistics taken last year show a different story.
Whereabouts? Was that not in the pools?
No; all along the river.
Does the minister say "all along the river"?
Yes.
I take exception to that.
Last year there were 1,072 salmon and 2,529 grilse caught in that portion where fishing with nets was restricted.
Has the minister the number caught in the pools, and how many pools are there?
No; I have not that information.
Were all the fish mentioned caught in pools?
I cannot give that information.
What are those figures based upon?
Upon reports from the inspectors.

The minister knows that
salmon are caught in pools by angling only.
You said they were caught both ways.

The hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy), who is not here this evening, has asked me to submit a question. He would like to know if the minister proposes to grant any subsidies to assist in the construction of barkentines which, I understand, are small schooners, along the Gaspe and Atlantic coasts?
There is no such intention.

I understand that a firm
known as the Canadian Cod Liver Oil Company, Limited, has established a plant at Rimouski to manufacture cod-liver oil. Has this company received any financial assistance in connection with the construction of the plant or the purchase of the land? What progress is being made at this plant? Has the minister given any consideration to the bonusing of the fishermen who supply cod-livers to the plant?

A plant to reduce cod-livers has been established at Rimouski in the province of Quebec, but this company has not received any subsidy or grant from the federal government. There has been no application made to the department for the payment of subsidies to fishermen who deliver livers to this plant, and I doubt if it would be possible. I understand that this company has a system of collecting the livers .along the coast and has centralized the reduction at Rimouski.
What amount has the plant produced up to the present time?
I have not that information.
