82.	Special. To provide for the extension of educational work in cooperative producing and selling among fishermen, $25,000.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words on item 82. I want to thank the minister for the grant he has given to the school of fisheries at Sainte-Anne-de-la-Pocatiere. That $8,000 grant from the Department of Fisheries has been very useful, for the last few years, to the fishermen of my constituency and to those of Gaspe. The technicians who belong to the teaching staff of the school of fisheries, and Mr. Alexandre Goudreau in particular, have organized throughout the Gaspe peninsula cooperatives which have been of immense advantage to our fishermen. I call this item in particular to the attention of the minister and I hope that the grant will be continued. Already the different cooperatives organized have 1,681 members belonging to 11 syndicates operating, thanks to the grant which the Minister of Fisheries has allocated to the school of fisheries of Sainte-Anne-de-la-Pocatiere for the last few years, and as the estimates have been reduced, I am afraid that the minister might reduce the grant. Should the minister discontinue or reduce the grant to the school of Sainte-Anne-de-la-Pocatiere, I fear that the cooperatives and the syndicates which have helped our fishermen to recover from a very difficult situation could not survive by their own means, as they are not strong enough yet. I beg the minister to show the same sympathy to the school of Sainte-Anne-de-la-Pocatiere and to continue the grant through which the cooperatives and syndicates of Gaspe have been developed to the point where they have sold last year over 6 million pounds of fillets.

1,9. National Housing Act, administration, $89,390.

I have the National Housing Act of 1938 before me and, according to the preamble "it is in the national interest that a limited experiment in low-rental housing should be undertaken now, creating needed employment and directing public attention to the importance of housing problems generally, and providing a basis of experience on which the provinces and municipalities may follow sound and proven policies in the future." Then by section 3 the minister, with the approval of the governor in council, may:
(a) carry on or arrange for the carrying on of investigations as to housing conditions and the adequacy of existing housing accommodation in Canada or any part of Canada and as to the best means to be adopted to improve housing conditions.
Would the minister make a statement regarding the position in Canada at the present time as a result of the work of the housing administration in accordance with section 3 (a) ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not prepared to deal adequately with that question to-night. The hon. gentleman is really asking me to give the committee a survey of housing conditions all over Canada. It would be a pretty lengthy undertaking, and I am not in a position to give it to-night.

I am sorry I was not in the house a week ago Monday when a discussion took place on the tax on building materials. To my mind, as I indicated when discussing the budget on May 7, housing is one of the most important national problems at the present time. If the minister cannot give this information to-night, would he agree to let this item stand until to-morrow and give the committee the information then?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman wants the information for himself I shall get it for him; but if he wants it for the House of Commons he is asking for it at a very inconvenient time in the session. His question would involve a survey of housing conditions throughout Canada, and to cover that would require a forty- or sixty-minute speech. Generally speaking, I may say that there is a war-time housing problem, and that is the immediate and pressing housing problem. That is being solved by War-time Housing Limited, which is a corporation set up by the Department of Munitions and Supply. The problem with which that corporation is concerning itself has not much to do with the National Housing Act.
The National Housing Act, as the hon. gentleman has stated, was passed at a time when there was unemployment in the country, and had as one of its objects the furnishing of employment and the encouragement of building because there was unemployment at that time. That particular reason no longer exists, although perhaps there are some other reasons why the housing act should be carried on. Consideration is being given from time to time to the National Housing Act. We have not yet terminated it; we are still carrying it on. It provides assistance to private builders of houses, and there is a considerable demand. On the other hand, it is just a question whether the government at a time like this should go into any expenditures or incur any obligation to assist in the private building of houses. The two problems are entirely separate. The war-time housing demand exists in localities where there has been a rapid expansion of war industry and where temporary housing would probably not be required after the war. That is one problem. The other is to assist persons to own their homes at reasonable prices with government assistance. That is another problem entirely, and we are certainly not extending the field of those operations. More and more people now are able to assume those responsibilities themselves.

I am still not satisfied
with the answer which the minister has given. I know that a war-time housing administra-

tion has been set up, but according to a return tabled on June 4 there were not any housing units completed up to May 1. Contracts had been let in Halifax, New Glasgow, Dartmouth, St. Catharines, Welland, Merritton, Hamilton, Fort Erie, Peterborough and Fort William. As I pointed out on May 7, I believe the government is not attaching sufficient importance to this phase of our war effort. On that occasion I mentioned that in the United States in the last war there was a wastage up to 10 per cent as a result of not having housing available in strategic centres. The Minister of Munitions and Supply stated this afternoon that we are embarking on a $400,000,000 munitions undertaking. Five per cent is a very conservative estimate in view of our serious housing shortage to-day compared with conditions at the beginning of the last war, because we have a surplus of possibly 1 per cent of houses in Canada to-day compared with 7 to 15 per cent of vacant houses at the beginning of the last war. Supposing there is a 5 per cent wastage, we are going to run into a tremendous outlay. We have set aside $10,000,000 for wartime housing, but I am not at all satisfied that the government are giving the direction to this problem which they should. The personnel of the directors would indicate that they are dollar-a-year men who are giving their services free of charge. As I pointed out the other day, I think we should have men, and women too, directing the affairs of this organization on a salary basis. In my opinion there are too many dollar-a-year men directing important undertakings.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on a point of order-and I am just asking for a ruling on this-is it not contrary to the rules of the house to permit a newspaper letter to be read in answer to a speech of a member of this house? I listened to the hon. senior member for Halifax the other day, and it was quite open, I should think, during that debate, and perhaps at the present time, for an hon. member to answer his speech, but to read a letter from a citizen of Halifax rebutting the speech of a member of this house, is, I believe, strictly against the rules.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
On the point of order,
it is not in order to read articles from newspapers or letters written by private persons outside the house. Some brief reference can be made to them, and to articles in newspapers, but it is an abuse if the whole article or a lengthy letter is read. If no exception is taken, sometimes it passes as a measure of latitude given to an hon. member. But it is

against the rales of the house to read articles from newspapers or private letters which originate elsewhere. Brief references to them may be made, but the reading of such documents is against the rule.

I am very glad to bow to your ruling, Mr. Chairman. I refrain from making further reference to this letter. I should like to urge hon. members to read the Halifax Chronicle of Wednesday, June 4, and see what a distinguished medical practitioner in the city of Halifax says about the urgent housing problems of that city. Since I am not permitted to proceed along that line, I wonder whether the minister would make a statement regarding section 3 (b):
. . . investigations as to plans or proposals that have been adopted elsewhere than in Canada. . . .
I should imagine that his national housing organization, in carrying out the provisions of this act before the war-time housing scheme was set up, would have instituted a survey of housing problems across Canada, and I do not think it is too much to ask the minister to give the committee the result of findings made by that administration to cope with an urgent problem.

I have listened
with great interest to what the hon. gentleman has had to say. I have been connected, as a matter of fact, with the Toronto housing company for a great many years. I thoroughly approve the stand which the government are taking to-day in connection with their temporary housing arrangements. I do not think this is an appropriate time for the government to spend money on permanent homes; the government need the money for war-time expenditures. I thoroughly approve the government's plan. Furthermore, these people who will be housed in various sections of the country owing to the contingencies of the moment will probably not remain in those districts after the war. Therefore we do not want to build up in the different communities a permanent provision for something which is not going to be permanent. I approve the plan of getting people to buy war savings stamps, invest in victory loans, and so forth. They will have something stored away, so that when the war is over they will be provided with some capital, will be able to return to the communities whence they came, and where permanent businesses will be established, and have some resources to go on with. Then, I believe, will be the time for the government to provide money for the construction of permanent homes.

If I may have the indulgence of the committee, because I must plead that I was a little deaf in missing the item when it came up, I should like to revert for a moment to item 46- I shall not occupy more than a minute or two.
Item 46 relates to a question of administration. I hold in my hand the report of the standing committee on banking and commerce, under date of Thursday, June 1, 1939. This committee was set up for the purpose of going into the monetary system of Canada, and it served a useful purpose. We had before us a great many witnesses, and those hon. members who sat on the committee had an opportunity to air their own particular theories and views. I am sure the minister will agree with me when I say that the meetings of that committee, at which we had evidence from such distinguished men as Mr. Graham Towers and Mr. Clark, have stopped a great deal of talking in the House of Commons by lion, members who know nothing whatever about banking or commerce. I admit that, having been a member of that committee, I did glean a little knowledge, and I think we got some idea of how little everybody knows about the monetary system to-day. I would refer to this statement in the committee's report:
Your committee has been unable in one session of parliament to complete its study of so wide a subject and recommends that the study of the subject be continued during future sessions of parliament.
All the members of the banking and commerce committee, the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Kinley), the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker), the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer) and all others, took an intense interest in the study which we carried out that time. We heard many witnesses, and a great deal of good was accomplished. I was going to make a suggestion. We have had a considerable amount of discussion on the budget. We have talked a great deal about it, and there are a good many members of the house-I saj' this with all due respect to all the members of the House of Commons including myself-who do not know everything. As a matter of fact, sometimes a good many of us have talked about things we do not know very much about. We are going to have to raise more money during the war, and my suggestion is that we have a meeting of the banking and commerce committee again along these lines.
I am sure the members of the committee will all be glad to serve on it and to give their time and talents to the work, with a 14S73

view to offering the minister suggestions which would help him in his work. We could study the monetary system and also the principles of taxation. I might refer the minister to a few remarks he made in connection with taxation. He admitted on several occasions that he was inexperienced, and I do not think that is to his discredit. He has done a marvellous job in a great many ways, and it is all the more credit to him to admit his inexperience in some matters. Not only that, but he has imposed certain taxes which he has had to take back, and I admire him for so doing.
At any rate, I believe that a good deal of controversy could be eliminated in the way I have suggested, if the banking and commerce committee were allowed to convene next October, or whenever we come back, and call witnesses.
The deputy minister in his report has given some outstanding information. I certainly give him credit for it. No one knows more about most of these matters than Mr. Towers, and his views were very useful. The trouble is, there are so many subjects connected with the question of taxation. It is a study in itself. The law of diminishing returns is something that must always be kept in view. I am not a student of economics, but I have a little common sense and that is all we need. Without disclosing any idea of what there was going to be in the budget, the minister would get a vast amount of information from all parts of the country, from all members of the committee. From my own observations in the banking and commerce committee I doubt very much if another body of men could be found in Canada with a broader knowledge of three things-human nature, psychology, and banking and business.
I would also compliment the chairman of the committee, who is an economist of no mean understanding. There are a great many men in this country whom we could have before us, who have their own ideas. We could find out many things that wrnuld be helpful. We could have before us people from various parts of Canada, the westerner and the easterner, expressing their respective points of view with regard to taxation. Principles would be discussed, and everything would be done without disclosing what the budget would contain. We could get the advantage of the best brains in the country.
The minister has been so frank in some of the statements he has made in connection with taxation that I would urge upon him the

importance of having the banking and commerce committee functioning. The minister knows how broad the whole subject is. I know the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg and all the other members of the committee will bear me out.

I wish to associate myself with the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Ross) in advocating that the banking and commerce committee be used for the purposes he has outlined. I am positive that before long the government will see its need to know more about money than it does at the present time; the most reactionary people will learn something progressive about money. I therefore take pleasure in supporting his proposal.

Under the national housing act a great deal of good work has been done in the outskirts of some of the larger cities; but during the debate the other night when reference was made to the administration of the act, and the details of the item on page 79 of the estimates, it was not pointed out that the whole thing grew out of what was done by the Bennett government when my motion for a housing committee was adopted. In 1935 a committee was appointed on this motion to consider the whole housing and reconstruction situation. It sat for three months and brought down a splendid lot of recommendations which resulted in the setting up of this act and a federal housing policy, and according to the figures given by the minister, something like $50,000,000 has been spent to date on it. One resolution which I myself proposed was adopted, namely, that the work should be done not by a government department but through the banks. The work has been well done, and I trust that, in view of the high cost of building, the need of small homes in cities and the high rates of interest- six and a half and six per cent, and some of the shark loan companies take bills of sale and chattel mortgages-the minister will take some steps to work out a continuing policy for the next few years of small houses which are badly needed.
There is some duplication in the administration of this department since the war started, and War-time Housing Limited is building these fabricated houses in Halifax and other places. I was looking over the situation in Toronto the other day, and I appreciate the work the department has done. I hope they will still continue and extend it, and take some measures through the banks or loan companies to advance money to these small wage earners, many of them munition workers, for the building of small houses. The Bruce

report on housing in Toronto did not build any houses; it got some tom down because the city amended the by-laws, but the city of Toronto was one of the pioneers in housing. I do not agree with what was said here some three weeks ago about Toronto. Toronto has no slums; it has a few dilapidated houses, but the statements made were totally incorrect. Anyone visiting the outskirts such as Leaside would see many excellent small houses. Travelling between Toronto and Muskoka and Parry Sound and other parts of new Ontario, one sees unsuitable dwellings. I hope this work will not be forgotten during war time because it is one of the most necessary things the government can do, and this department has done good work.
Would the minister answer my question about the survey work carried on by this department prior to the setting up of War-time Housing Limited? .

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The national housing administration ever since it was set up has been making surveys in various parts of the dominion so as to acquaint itself with housing needs. That is in the ordinary course of its work in administering the National Housing Act. The surveys they made, the information they gathered, were of value to the government when the government was formulating its policy with regard to war-time housing. The government has full appreciation of the importance of supplying housing, seeing that temporary housing is furnished for these war industry centres, Halifax for example. But as I said, that is a different field of activity from that of the national housing administration. The tendency will be not to extend the national housing administration activities, but the acute housing problem in various parts of the dominion brought about by war conditions is being attended to by War-time Housing Limited, which is under the department of my colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply, not the Department of Finance.

According to an order in council passed on February 24 set out in section 4, paragraph (c), it would be the duty of War-time Housing Limited to draw upon the personnel and other technical resources relating to housing at present in the government service, and in particular to utilize the services of the housing branch of the Department of Finance. In the order for return part of my question was:
Were members of the staff of national housing moved to Toronto and later brought back to Ottawa? If so, for what reason?

Supply-Finance-Housing Act
And the answer to that was:
Some members of the housing administration, Department of Finance, were temporarily moved to Toronto to assist in the organization of War-time Housing Limited. When their services were no longer required in this connection they returned to Ottawa to the housing administration.
Would the minister explain the relationship between those two departments? Why were some sent to Toronto and then called back, and what is their present position?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: At the present time there is no relationship between them, except that national housing administration is making available information they gathered. But employees of the national housing branch are not now working for or in War-time Housing Limited. War-time Housing Limited has perfected its own organization, and the initial assistance which it received from Mr. Nieolls and this branch has ceased. The employees who went to Halifax to assist at the beginning have come back to Ottawa, and the two organizations are now separate.

From the speech the minister made on June 2, I gather that he plans on national housing going out of business. He indicated that while national housing activities are all right in peace time, now the job should be done by war-time housing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are two different jobs. I did not, I think, say anything to the contrary on June 2. I have said that the tendency is to curtail and not expand: the activities of the housing branch, but that is different from going out of business. The hon. gentleman must realize that they have a tremendous job to do in any event with regard to the present investment the government -has in all parts of the country in housing. No decision has been reached to cease further advances under the National Housing Act.

I understand -that the rules prevent me from reading from previous debates, but the minister's reference on June 2, carried to its logical -conclusion, would mean that national housing would automatically fold up for the duration of the war. I have been trying for six weeks to get information as -to what War-time Housing Limited is doing, and I think the minister's department, the Department of Pensions and National Health, which has also done a good deal on the housing question in Canada, and the national research council, which has carried on very valuable research work, should be used by War-time Housing Limited.
I referred to this order in council passed on February 24, and I find that another order
in council passed later, on April 24, rescinds that very important section. Would the minister explain what is happening? I think it was good business to pass the order in council of February 24 saying that-
... it may draw upon the -personnel and upon the economic and other technical resources relating to housing presently available in the government service, and in particular shall utilize the services of the housing branch of the Department of Finance.
Therefore some explanation should be given why it was decided on April 24 to reverse that policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I gave the explanation. The employees of the national housing branch assisted War-time Housing Limited in the initial stages. Then it was decided by Waintime Housing Limited that it would be preferable for them to go on with their own organization, not using the employees of another branch of the government. By mutual consent it was decided that those employees should return and continue in the employ of the national housing branch.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health

Might I intervene to say that by consent it has been arranged to sit until midnight. Therefore a formal motion will not be

How long was the staff of his department setting up War-time Housing Limited? How long did they work?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Some of them were in Toronto nearly a month; some, not so long.

I realize that members of the committee are anxious to complete the business, and I certainly would not take the time of the committee unless I considered that this was an urgent question which is not receiving the consideration on the part of the government that it deserves.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member is wrong about that, I can assure him.

There are three departments of government which have given important consideration to this problem. My information is that their services are not being used by War-time Housing Limited. I refer to the
Supply-Finance-Housing Act

Department of Pensions and National Health. I have before me a pamphlet they produced in 1938. It indicates that they have made a careful study of the whole question of housing, as it relates to the public health of Canada. I commend the department for this excellent publication. The bureau of national research has carried on scientific work in this field. My information is that their research facilities and their services are not being used by War-time Housing Limited.
The minister has not satisfied me so far as to why this order in council was passed on February 24, requiring the personnel of the national housing administration to be used by War-time Housing Limited. These are men who had training in their particular field. They are men over whom we have some control. Goggin as general manager at $10,000 a year. I suggest that this procedure does not establish confidence in the minds of the people who have been interested in this problem.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member is discussing the hiring of a man by War-time Housing Limited. That has nothing to do with the subject matter before the committee. Whether or not the Department of Munitions and Supply has hired a man at a salary of $10,000 is not relevant, so far as the present item is concerned. It might be considered when we are discussing the estimates of the Department of Munitions and Supply.
As I understand it, the hon. member is asking why the organization already in existence has not been used, and why another organization has been set up. That is his point.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, I know. I have answered the point, as best I can. I have told about the beginning of the activities of War-time Housing Limited in Toronto. I have told how Mr. Nicolls assisted in the initial stages. I have described how it was decided, by mutual consent-certainly it was the opinion of Wartime Housing Limited, and I believe it was also the opinion of Mr. Nicolls-that it would be better if War-time Housing Limited got together its own staff and its own organization, thereby permitting Mr. Nicolls' staff to return to Ottawa. They had plenty of work to do, themselves.
It was considered desirable that those two organizations continue separately, instead of together. Because the terms of the order in council seemed to make it obligatory upon

the members of the national housing administration, the employees of the national housing branch, to serve in War-time Housing Limited -something which War-time Housing Limited, after a trial, considered undesirable, and a consideration in which Mr. Nicolls concurred- the change in the order in council was made.

I believe hon. members in all parts of the house are proud of the accomplishments of the national housing administration. The minister stated that prior to the setting up of War-time Housing Limited, a survey had been made regarding needs in Canada. That was part of the routine work of national housing. Can the minister give any good reason why the national housing administration could not have gone on and carried out the work now being undertaken by War-time Housing Limited? Could it not have done that work more efficiently and more economically for the Canadian taxpayer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a different matter altogether. They could not do both.
Why not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Because they have too much to do in the national housing end of the work. The national housing branch has a long-term and a steady job, of a particular type. They are working on one problem, while War-time Housing Limited is dealing with a temporary and a different type of problem altogether. It is dealing with temporary, government-built and government-owned houses. Other houses are not government-built or government-owned. They are permanent houses, privately built, with government assistance by way of loans. It is a different matter entirely.
We felt that the building of temporary houses was a war-time problem, a temporary problem, and one of the type for which the Department of Munitions and Supply was designed. The Department of Munitions and Supply did take charge of the problem. They used our employees for a while and, under circumstances I have indicated to the committee, they decided that it would be better for them to go on with their own organization, completely, and to let the national housing administration continue with its good work.

If I understood the minister correctly, he pointed out that before War-time Housing Limited was set up, the national housing administration went to those points where there were acute housing problems, and carried out their survey work.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes.

Supply-Finance-Housing Act

Were they not making a plan to deal with this problem? Were they not changing national housing activities so that they could enter the field of pre-fabricated houses, or temporary houses? Was there any definite reason why the national housing administration might not enter the temporary housing field, and do it more economically and more efficiently than Wartime Housing Limited?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was thought they could not.	.
Why?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They may have had plans to do that, but it was decided by the government that the other plan would be the better way of doing it.

I say that the minister is handing over 810,000,000 which should be given to the national housing administration. That is something to think about, and something which ought to be the concern of this committeg. I realize that a discussion of War-time Housing Limited activity does not come under this vote, and I must bow to the ruling of the Chair. But I suggest that the minister of this department has something to answer for.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of this department, do you say?
Yes, the department of the Minister of Finance has something to answer for in failing to keeping the activities under a government-controlled organization-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no ambition to take charge of war-time housing, I can assure the hon. member. It is not the function of the Minister of Finance to regulate housing. In this instance its functions are predominantly those of lending, on good credit.
And you are still going to lend.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: So long as we carry on the administration of the National Housing Act. We administer that act which has to do, mainly, with the lending of money to private individuals. That is a different matter altogether from building houses. Even if I had the power, I would not let the Department of Finance go into the business of building government houses.
But the Minister of Finance is going to hand over 810,000,000 of the taxpayers' money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
To War-Time Housing Limited?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

I think it would be
much better to have that 810,000,000 spent under the minister's supervision, on a lending basis, if necessary, for the use of corporations which are going to need additional housing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I disagree.

Does not the hon.
member realize that he has 'been, discussing War-Time Housing Limited? We are not discussing the National Housing Act in the terms he has indicated. 50. Old age pensions, including pensions to the blind, administration, $42,320.

Has any consideration been given to the provision of some sort of cost of living bonus for old-age pensioners? I realize there will have to be some discussion with or endorsation by the provinces-at least, I presume there will have to be because they pay a portion of the old age pension. We find in our districts that these old people are suffering a great deal because of the increased cost of living, while their pensions remain strictly limited. I suggest that this problem should receive the serious consideration of the government, particularly in view of the fact that Canada is the most backward country in the British empire with regard to old age pensions and general security legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have received quite a number of representations, but we have not taken any action nor have we given the matter extended consideration. It would require an amendment to the act to raise the amount beyond 820 a month, and there would have to be new agreements with all the provinces. The cost of living has not advanced more than 7 or 8 per cent since the outbreak of the war, and I do not think there would be a sound reason for amending the act and entering into new agreements.
Has the government received any representation from any of the provincial governments?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not so far as I can recall; I think they have all been from private individuals and organizations.

Is the government willing to negotiate with the provinces?
Supply-Finance-Housing Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I could not say, because the question has not been considered by the government. I am more than doubtful about the provinces being willing to do it although I have no definite information on that.

Did the minister say that
he had received no representation from any of the provinces, from British Columbia, for instance?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think any representation has been received from any provincial government.

My impression is that the
matter was discussed in the local house and that a resolution was passed, but I may be wrong. I noticed in the papers yesterday that the electric railway men in the home town of the hon. member for Vancouver South have been given a wage increase of six cents an hour, which works out more nearly to a 12 per cent increase than 6 or 7 or 10 per cent. A 10 per cent increase on the $20 would be $2. That may not seem much to us, but it would mean a great deal to these old people. We have only to look across the line at Washington where for some time they have been receiving something like $30 a month.

This is a matter of great concern to the old people of Canada. If we take the dominion as a whole, at least 50 per cent of the population over seventy years of age are in receipt of old age pensions. This pension of $20 a month provides only for a niggardly means of sustenance. The average pension received does not amount to $20 a month. A return tabled a few weeks ago by the Minister of Finance gives the following average pensions:
Alberta	 $18.56
British Columbia	 19.12
Manitoba	 18.70
New Brunswick	 14.65
Nova Scotia	 14.92
Ontario	 18.56
Prince Edward Island	 11.32
Quebec	 15.66
Saskatchewan	 16.93
Northwest Territories	 20.00
It is only in the Northwest Territories that the full pension is paid. The minister said that the cost of living has risen some 7 or 8 per cent. The papers to-day give the figure as being almost eight per cent. The old age pension received in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Quebec and Saskatchewan is $15 or less, and 8 per cent of $15 would be $1.20. What it really amounts to is that, instead of getting $15 a month, these old people are getting less than $14 a month.
We are making provision for the payment of bonuses to people in industry. In many 
instances this is being done, not to make adjustments, not because we think they should have it, but because we are afraid if they do not get it they will make trouble. Surely we should not overlook these old people who are not in a position to make trouble, who must take what they can get and get along with it. When, as was pointed out a moment ago, the government can provide $10,000 a year for a man who is going to do something that we do not know about as yet, surely it can do something for the old people of this country.

I should like to associate
myself with those hon. members who have spoken on this subject. I have spoken on it quite often in the past, but apparently with no success. I should like to make a few remarks because I think this matter has an important bearing upon the economy of this country. As the hon. member for Vancouver South has said, Canada lags behind every other country in the British empire in the matter of old age pensions, both as to the age limit and as to the amount. I do not know why the age limit is set at seventy years, unless it be that according to the good book, if a man is not dead at seventy, he ought to be.

They do not think he
will live long after that.

Small as the maximum
pension is, most of the recipients receive even less. I have often wondered why Canada lags behind in old age pensions. There are psychological reasons. I believe it is because we are supposed to be a thrifty people. It is thought that if a man has been a virtuous citizen he should be able to provide for his old age. If he has not been able to do so, then he should be punished for his sins in the past. Originally thrift meant putting a thing to its best use, but to-day it means nothing more or less than saving money. I tried to prove in the committee on banking and commerce, but in vain, that no man can save money except at the expense of the community. It is bound to cause a shortage in purchasing power. What is the purpose of this drive to encourage savings, if not to decrease purchasing power? The reason for this is the war, but the war will not last forever. I want to be on record with regard to this matter.
I can only hope that the policy we followed after the last war, that of deflation, will not be followed after this war is won. We shall have to do the opposite, and I do not know a better way of putting out fresh purchasing

Supply-Finance-Housing Act
power than through the old age pensions, by increasing the amount of the pension and by lowering the age at which it is payable.
For those who might object to my statement that an individual saves money only at the expense of the community, let me put it in this way: If a man saves money he is producing more than he is consuming-I think there can be no argument about that-or he is selling more than he is buying. If he succeeds in doing that, someone somewhere must be buying more than he is selling, and the unemployment problem in all countries is partly due to this craving for saving money. For the benefit of those who do not agree with these ideas, let me quote briefly from "Essays in Persuasion" by John Maynard Keynes. He says this on that subject:
There are to-day many well-wishers of their country who believe that the most useful thing which they and their neighbours can do to mend the situation is to save more than usual.
This was written in 1932, and at that time there was a depression, which we are promised we shall have when this war is over-unemployment and depression. Keynes wrote in similar circumstances after the last war. He goes on:
If they refrain from spending a larger proportion of their incomes than usual they believe that they will have helped employment. If they are members of town or county councils they believe that their right course at such a time as this is to oppose expenditure on new amenities or new public works.
Now, in certain circumstances all this would be quite right, but in present circumstances, unluckily, it is quite wrong. It is utterly harmful and misguided-the very opposite of the truth. For the object of saving is to release labour for employment on producing capital goods such as houses, factories, roads, machines, and the like. But if there is a large unemployed surplus already available for such purposes, then the effect of saving is merely to add to this surplus and therefore to increase the number of the unemployed. Moreover, when a man is thrown out of work in this or any other way, his diminished spending power causes further unemployment amongst those who would have produced what he can no longer afford to buy. And so the position gets worse and worse in a vicious circle.
The best guess I can make is that whenever you save five shillings, you put a man out of work for a day. Your saving that five shillings adds to unemployment to the extent of one man for one day-and so on in proportion.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. gentleman can make a brief reference to the text, but surely he cannot read page after page of a book.

I have not read a page
yet, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry but-
I have only three lines more, and I think it is a pity to spoil this quotation.
What book is my hon. friend reading from?

It is "Essays in Persuasion" by John Maynard Keynes, an economist of some note and not a Social Crediter. Great minds think alike, as I may remind the hon. gentlemen. To conclude this quotation:
On the other hand, whenever you buy goods you increase employment-though they must be British, home-produced goods if you are to increase employment in this country. After all, this is only the plainest common sense. For if you buy goods, some one will have to make them. And if you do not buy goods, the shops will not clear their stocks, they will not give repeat orders, and some one will be thrown out of work.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member has crowded a lot of material into three lines.
He lost his place and found another one.

Yes; I missed my place and I think I read one part over twice. This passage seems to cause some merriment, but let me put this to hon. members. What was the position of this country before this war started as a result of the policies which they evidently still believe in? The Prime Minister of Great Britain said, "Never did so many owe so much to so few," and that applies to us in this country just as much as to anybody else. I say that the policies of deflation which were adopted after the last war not only made this war inevitable but made it impossible for those countries which followed these policies, and stayed with them to provide themselves with adequate protection.

When the estimates of the Minister of Mines and Resources were before the committee, I drew his attention to the fact that persons who had lived in the Yukon and had removed to other provinces were not entitled to count their residence in the Yukon for pension purposes in the province to which they removed, and that this causes a serious hardship to a comparatively small number of aged people. I was hoping that some consideration might be given to straightening out that difficulty and relieving these few aged people of the distress which is thereby caused. I am not going into particulars of this case because I mentioned it the other evening, and no doubt it has been brought to the attention of the department.
I thoroughly endorse the requests of those who to-night have asked for a bonus, or, what is better still, an increase for the aged people who are in receipt of the pension. The cost of living is going up. The staple articles which they use have gone up in price, and the new

Supply-Finance-Housing Act
taxes on sugar and on other commodities containing sugar still further increase the cost of living for these aged people and the blind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If I may interrupt for a moment, is it not true that a dollar will now buy more than it would in 1927 when the Old Age Pension Act was enacted?

It depends upon how you spend the dollar. So far as foodstuffs go, the minister is probably right. But that does not alter the fact that the pension is insufficient. May I point out that we have a very large number of people in Canada in receipt of old age pensions. I have here a copy of the report on the administration of old age pensions and pensions for the blind in Canada for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1941, and I find that we have altogether 185,946 pensioners, old age and blind. To me it is a striking commentary on our economy and on the economy of certain provinces to look over the list and note the percentage of pensioners in the various provinces. When I went west thirty-one yecrs ago I remember how at that time we thought we were going to a new land where in later years there would 'be security for all who toiled there. But when I look at the figures for Saskatchewan I find that 59-6 of all persons over seventy years of age are in receipt of an old age pension. In Alberta the percentage is 56-56; in Manitoba, 55-33 per cent; in British Columbia, 49-79 per cent; in Nova Scotia, 51-62 per cent. The worst, of course, is New Brunswick, with 61-83 per cent of all persons over seventy years of age in receipt of old age pensions.
There is another factor which ought to be considered. I was speaking this afternoon about the necessity of maintaining morale in ihis country, and I believe that morale depends to a very large extent upon the home conditions and the security of the people of our land. If we are going to give that security when the war is over, we might offer some indication of it now by giving the old age pensioners some increase, at least, of their pensions. This is being done in other parts of the British commonwealth. The motherland, with all her tremendous financial undertakings and obligations, has raised the old age pension quite substantially in the last year or so. New Zealand has done the same. But we in this country have not given any indication to our people that we have in mind anything but returning when this war is over to the old pre-war conditions. It is not good enough, and it is undermining the morale of our people.

I suggest that here is one place where we could show the people of Canada that we have something better in mind, by increasing for the old folks the comparatively small pensions which they now receive. I associate myself with all those who in this chamber have made this plea to-night.

Would the minister be
willing to open negotiations with the provinces concerning the question of paying such an increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is primarily a provincial responsibility.
Oh, no, it is not. The dominion pays 75 per cent; it is primarily a federal responsibility, and it cannot be shoved off on the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no; the provinces pay the pensioners and administer the system, and we make a grant.
They administer it, but the dominion pays 75 per cent of the amount, and certainly the provinces caifnot make a move without the help of the dominion.
And the auditor general has the last say.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is primarily provincial. They administer the system and pay the pensions, and we make a contribution.

Yes; but the pensioners are paid with the approval of the auditor general. If the province grants a pension, and the auditor general believes that the proof of age, for example, is insufficient, although the province has accepted it, the auditor general has the last word and turns down the pension. It would seem to be true that the province does administer it locally, but the final say and certainly the heavier responsibility are in the hands of the dominion government.

I would point out to the minister, as regards responsibility, that while, according to the British North America Act, it may originate in the province, yet it is a matter of record that, when we here passed the Old Age Pension Act, in 1927, it was the dominion that approached the provinces, and not the provinces the dominion, asking them whether they would "come through" if the dominion paid a certain portion. I remember that distinctly, because the question was asked here, and the minister made a reply stating how many provinces had replied to the invitation, and what their answers were. There is no question that the initiative did come on that occasion from the dominion.

Mr. GREEN; Is that part of the arrangement with regard to income tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Are not these votes which are now being deleted special subsidies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Were they covered by the offer to the provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Oh, yes. These are special grants, and all these are to be dropped with the
provinces which accept the offer, and all these provinces have indicated their intention of doing so.

Motion agreed to.
62.	Miscellaneous grants and contributions. To provide for report on cultural conditions in Canada (literature, art, drama, education, etc.), $2,500.
Is this necessary?
Would the minister explain to whom this item is to be paid, and what it is for?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This item has been here for some years. It is really a pension or grant for the benefit of a distinguished Canadian who has rendered a great service to Canada in the realm of literature. Questions are usually not pressed beyond that, on this item.

Item agreed to.
63.	Miscellaneous grants and contributions. Federal district commission-maintenance and improvement of grounds adjoining government buildings, Ottawa, and for improvements to the parkway system under the control of the federal district commission, $133,500.

This vote is for maintenance and improvement of grounds adjoining gov-erment buildings, Ottawa, and for improvements to the parkways system under the control of the federal district commission. Then there is an item for maintenance of parks, parkways and plant, Ottawa and vicinity under control of the federal district commission, and another item for the corporation of the city of Ottawa. The amounts for these three items are, respectively, $133,500, $200,000, and $100,000. Other municipalities do a considerable amount of similar work and do not get anything for it.
I would ask the minister whether consideration could not be given to a rearrangement of the monuments around these grounds. The monument to Sir John A. Macdonald is away at the back and Alexander Mackenzie is supposed to sleep on the strong box-I do not know if the minister guards it as closely- and D'Arcy McGee is in the backyard. I asked the Minister of Public Works about this matter last year, and I also discussed the question when my former leader, Mr. Bennett, was here. I thought there should be some rearrangement of these monuments in view of the changed situation in connection with the Canadian National station. Sir Wilfrid Laurier is in the front, and I am glad to see him there, but I suggest that in the recess the government might consult a landscape artist about this matter, because these
Supply-Finance

monuments are not very creditable to the present arrangement. Some are, as I say, in the backyard, some on the main street, and some obscured by a number of motor cars. In view of the ceremonies held at Kingston last Saturday, I suggest that some better position should be given the monument which was erected to the chief author of confederation, Sir John A. Macdonald, more in keeping with the prominent part he played in confederation and afterwards. I hope the government will take this matter up and try to beautify the grounds so as to have them harmonize better with the general surroundings, in view of the amount of money that has been spent. We are spending a great deal on purely municipal work while other places are entitled to consideration. I would ask the minister to give his consideration to this whole question and to consult the Minister of Public Works.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will bring the hon. member's request to the attention of the Minister of Public Works.
What does the word "vicinity" mean in connection with statutory vote for the federal district commission? Do we go much beyond the city limits?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is a district under the control of the federal district commission.
What is the mileage?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are parts of Hull and parts of Rockcliffe under the control of the commission.

Could the minister induce the city to do some better sanding, putting some calcium chloride in the sand? Round parliament buildings and the main streets of Ottawa it is terrible in the winter for cars as well as for people crossing the streets.
The hon. member must be a tenderfoot.
No matter who you are, you have to have creepers on.
Cannot some saving be made on this maintenance item?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A very large cut has been made in it.

Item agreed to.
67. General. To provide, subject to the approval of the treasury board, for salaries, reclassifications and increases, $100,000.

Will the minister explau,
this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is a continuation of a similar provision made in previous years to provide for salaries and increases for which provision is not made elsewhere in the estimates. It is intended to cover unforeseen contingencies that may arise with respect to staff and to avoid the possibility of crippling essential services. Allocations are made by the treasury board as required during the year.
Mr, NICHOLSON: How much was spent last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: All for the finance department?

66. General. Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, 1934, and Municipal Improvements Assistance Act, 1938, administration, $261,000.

What is the cost of the operation of the Municipal Improvements
Assistance Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The cost of administering the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act is almost infinitesimal. There is practically no staff at all. We are not making loans under that act.
How many cases were taken up in the last year, and what was the total amount adjusted?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
For the fiscal year ended
March 31, 1941, the number of farmers interviewing official receivers was 3,514; proposals submitted, 1,808; meetings of creditors held, 1,925; voluntary settlements effected by official receivers, 348; cases dealt with by boards of review, 3,418; total number of eases dealt with, 3,766.
The boards of review dealt with 3,418 cases in 1941. How does that compare with the previous year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In the previous year the
number was 6,162.
Then there is a falling [DOT] off of almost 50 per cent in the number of cases dealt with?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Thereabouts.

Is there any disposition on the part of the government to close up the boards of review and wind up their
operations?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think we could do that; there are still a good many cases to be attended to.

Supply-Auditor General's Office
Has the minister received any request in connection with the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act with regard to Manitoba?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

What consideration has been
given to it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Much consideration has
been given, but it was decided not to introduce any amendment before we adjourn this time at any rate.

68. General. Unforeseen expenses, expenditure thereof to be subject to the approval of the treasury board, and a detailed statement to be laid before parliament within fifteen days of next session, $80,000.
I should like an explanation of the words, "a detailed statement to be laid before parliament within fifteen days of next session." Does it mean within fifteen days after the session is opened?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.

How much was spent
last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Up to February 20, 1941,
the amount spent was $32,827. That is in the fiscal year 1940-41. After that, $1,271 was spent, making about $34,000 in all.

Item agreed to.
AUDITOR general's OFFICE
S3. Salaries and expenses of office, $455,790.
What is the relationship between the auditor general's department and the special government-owned corporations set up by the government in connection with war-time business?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are all audited by the auditor general just as if they were branches of departments of the government.

What is the reason for
eliminating from the auditor general's report a vast number of items, the doing of which has materially reduced the value of the report from the point of view of searches by members into statements?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There was an explanation
given in the report at page 561, but perhaps that was not considered sufficiently explanatory. Here is some further explanation.
Up to last year the report mingled English and French versions in the same volumes. In size the pages totalled 1,354. Last year separate volumes in each language were issued. These totalled 1,137 pages.
The act states what information must be included in the auditor general's report, but leaves to him the form in which it is to be presented. As a result the predecessor of the present auditor general stated in his report for 1923-24, page xx volume 1, that he had reduced the size by 1,000 pages that year. In the report for 1925-26 he advised that he had again reduced the size from 2,260 pages to 1,694, and further reductions were subsequently made, for the last report prior to that signed by the present auditor general consisted of 1,354 pages.
The auditor general says that what he did was to save over 130 pages when information supplied was duplicated elsewhere in the report. He also dropped certain tables of a statistical nature when the information is provided in other official reports, for example the tables of outstanding loan issues, because that information is to be found in the public accounts, also certain statistical tables which might be queried. One was that listing payments to newspapers, because, since much advertising is placed through advertising agencies, who receive commissions from the newspapers, the precise amount actually paid to a paper may not be that included in the statement.
The form is not always readily comparable with the report of the year before. Apparently it is within the discretion of the auditor general as to the form in which he puts his report, and he felt that he was saving duplication.

The title of the auditor general's department is not properly descriptive. Does the auditor general's office audit all war-time expenditures? As I understand it, the Department of National Defence and others have their own auditors, and the auditor general is an auditor of auditors. Does this office, costing $455,790 a year, audit all the government's war expenditures? I understand that each department dealing with all these outside boards and dollar-a-year men and all the departments, fifty-six of them, have auditors themselves. Doer the auditor general re-audit them or lay down rules for the audit by the sub-auditors of the various departments? Does the auditor general supervise all the war expenditures that have been gone over by some roving committees of the House of Commons?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know that I can give a quick description of exactly what he does. The comptroller of the treasury, representing the Minister of Finance, has his officers, who are numerous, in every branch of the government service, and sees to it that money is not spent unless duly authorized.

Senate and House of Commons
The auditor general's function is that of a representative of parliament. He is responsible to parliament, not to the government. He supervises and audits here and there throughout the whole government service, and reports to parliament.
I presume this vote covers the peace-time activities only. Has the minister available the additional amount required to look after war-time activities?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is some vote authorized out of the war appropriations. I have not the amount here. I am sure it has been given to the house at an earlier time.

I should like to say a word in support of the argument of the hon. member for Davenport. The remarks regarding the saving by the auditor general may be correct, and of course cutting out duplication is all to the good. But so far as the average member of parliament is concerned, practically the whole usefulness of the report is destroyed. Time was when if someone came along and said that Tom Jones was getting too big a salary or too much in his expense account, one could look him up and find exactly what pay lie was drawing and what expenses. Now one cannot do that. One can go to the auditor general's office as I have done, and he was courtesy itself and gave me a great deal of information about the particular man, but what I want is to be able to check up on any man in the government service. It very often stops claims that a man is being heayily overpaid, and I used to appreciate it very much, but now the auditor general's report is of no value at all from that point of view.
Item stands.
Progress reported.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That the said amendment be now read the second time and concurred in; but that this house, while disapproving of any infraction of its privileges or rights by the other house, in this case waives its claims to insist upon such rights and privileges; but the waiver of the said rights arid privileges is not to be drawn into a precedent; and, further, that this house agrees to the incorporation in this bill of Bill No. 101, an act to amend the Special War Revenue Act,
And that a message be sent to the senate to acquaint their honours therewith.
He said: The amendment made by the other house to the Special War Revenue Act is very

small in relation to the revenue collected. It is scarcely a revenue amendment. The amendment proposes a change in a section of the act. The suggestion is that proclamation of coming into force is not to be made until their constitutionality is submitted to the Supreme Court of Canada. As I had agreed that immediately these sections were passed-if they were passed-they would be submitted to the Supreme Court of Canada anyway, I am making this motion now, but asserting the principle that this house is waiving none of its privileges with regard to money amendments.

Motion agreed to, amendment read the second time and concurred in.
